macung, e; f. Making, doing, action :-- Þurh ðes macunge m&aelig-acute;st se eorl Rotbert ðises geáres ðis land mid unfriþe gesóhte it was mostly his doing that Earl Robert attacked this country in the course of this year, Chr. 1101; Erl. 238, 1.
mád (v. ge-maad vecors, Wrt. Voc. ii. 123, 36); adj. Unreasoning, foolish, mad :-- Þrinteþ him on innan ungeméde mád mód within him (one guilty of oferhygd) swells a mind displeasing by its folly, Exon. 83 b; Th. 315, 2; Mód. 25. v. ge-m&aelig-acute;d.
mádm. v. máðm.
m&aelig-acute;, more. v. má.
mæc; adj. Well-matched, equal, agreeable(?) :-- Hár hildering hréman ne þorfte macan (other MSS. mecca, meca, mecga) gem&aelig-acute;nan the grey-haired warrior had no need to boast of well-matched intercourse, i. e. would not boast of being a match for those against whom he fought, and by whom he had been defeated, Chr. 937; Erl. 114, 6; Ædelst. 40. [Prompt. Parv. make or fyte and mete; mak, fyt, esy aptus, conveniens : Icel. makr suitable, easy to deal with.] v. ge-mæc.
mæced [ = má-éced? cf. má-geéct] glosses mactus, Wrt. Voc. ii. 79, 53.
Mæcedonie; pl. The Macedonians :-- Philippus Mæcedonia cyning, Ors. 4, 11; Swt. 204, 5. Gewin wið Mæcedonie, Swt. 202, 33.
Mæcedonisc; adj. Macedonian :-- Ðæt Mæcedonisce gewin, Ors. 4, 11; Swt. 208, 5.
m&aelig-acute;ce-fisc. v. méce-fisc.
mæcg,mecg, es; m. A man :-- Ic meþelcwide mæcges (the angel that visited Guthlac) ongeat, Exon. 50 b; Th. 175, 9; Gú. 1192. Mægþ and mæcgas, 45 a; Th. 153. 29; Gú. 833 : 113 a; Th. 434, 7; Rä. 51, 7. Fréfra ðíne mæcgas (the disciples of St. Andrew), Andr. Kmbl. 843; An. 422. Mæcga misgehýd men's evil intent, 1543; An. 773. Mæcgea (mecga, MS. C.) mundbora (Edmund), Chr. 942; Erl. 116, 8, Mecga (those in hell) gnornunge,Cd. 220; Th. 285, 8; Sat. 334. Mæcgum (the children in the fiery furnace), 187; Th. 232, 24; Dan. 265. Adam iécte siððan mægþum and mæcgum m&aelig-acute;gburg síne Adam afterwards increased his family with daughters and sons, 55; Th. 68, 26; Gen. 1123. DER. ambeht-, earfoþ-, eóred-, Geát-, gigant-, here-, hilde-, oret-,wræc-mæcg.
MÆCGA - M&AElig-acute;G-CWEALM
mæcga, an; m. A man, Exon. 88 a; Th. 330, 16; Vy. 52. v. gúþ-, ofer-, wræc-mæcga.
mæcige, Lchdm. iii. 126, 19. v. mecgan.
mæctor. v. m&aelig-acute;te.
M&AElig-acute;D, e and we; m&aelig-acute;dwe, an; f. also (?) m&aelig-acute;dwa, an; m. A MEAD, meadow :-- M&aelig-acute;d pratum, Ælfc. Gl. 57; Som. 67, 75; Wrt. Voc. 38, 1 : 96; Som. 76, 45; Wrt. Voc. 53, 52. xii æcras an westhealfe ðære str&aelig-acute;te and án médwa beneoþan ðæm hliþe xii acres on the west side of the road, and one meadow beneath the hill, Cod. Dipl. Kmbl. iii. 52, 15. vi æcras m&aelig-acute;de on ða geréfm&aelig-acute;de, 53, 2. xvi gioc ærþelandes and médwe, i. 316, 26. On Wíferþes m&aelig-acute;duan hege to the hedge of Wiferth's meadow, iii. 78, 21. Andlang heges on Eomeres m&aelig-acute;duan (cf. on Eomeres médwa, 405, 24) ; of ðam m&aelig-acute;duan . . . andlang burnan on Hereferþes m&aelig-acute;duan, 78, 6-9. Tó wudum&aelig-acute;dwan; of ðæm m&aelig-acute;dwan, 246, 22. (In the last two passages perhaps the forms are plural as in) Tó ð&aelig-acute;m m&aelig-acute;dwum wið súðan ða m&aelig-acute;dwa, 169, 2-3. [Mid l&aelig-acute;swe and mid m&aelig-acute;dwe, Chr. 777; Erl. 55, 12.] Gelíce and mon m&aelig-acute;d máwe just as one mows a meadow, Ors. 2, 8; Swt. 92, 15. xiiii æceras and ða m&aelig-acute;de ðe ðár tó líþ Ðúnstán gebohte æt Uhtlufe xiiii acres and the meadow pertaining thereto Dunstan bought of Uhtlufu, Cod. Dipl. Kmbl. ii. 3, 34. Norþrihte on m&aelig-acute;re m&aelig-acute;de westewearde, iii. 416, 18. Of ðere ealdan díc ðæt on wylihte m&aelig-acute;dwan; of wylihte m&aelig-acute;dwan, 235, 16. On rýdm&aelig-acute;dwan ufewarde, 378, 14. Eahta æceras m&aelig-acute;dwa . . . xii æceras m&aelig-acute;dwa, 4, 12-13. M&aelig-acute;da prata, Hpt. Gl. 409, 38. Ðeós wyrt biþ cenned on m&aelig-acute;dum this plant is produced in meadows, Herb. 1, 1; Lchdm. i. 70, 2. [Cf. Ger. mähde a meadow.] v. gafol-, geréf-, mór-m&aelig-acute;d; m&aelig-acute;þ.
m&aelig-acute;d, m&aelig-acute;dan. v. ge-m&aelig-acute;d, ge-m&aelig-acute;dan.
m&aelig-acute;den. v. mægden.
mæder (?), a measure :-- Ofgeót mid. iii. mædrum ealoþ, Lchdm. iii. 28, 16.
mædere, an; f. Madder :-- Mæddre vermiculi, rubia, Ælfc. Gl. 42; Som. 64, 13, 19; Wrt. Voc. 31, 24, 29. Mædere anchorum, 67, 38 : veneria, 68, 38 : sandix (herba), Hpt. Gl. 524, 41. Ðeós wyrt ðe man gryas and óðrum naman mædere nemneþ, Herb. 51, 1; Lchdm. i. 154, 12 : L. M. 2, 51; Lchdm. ii. 268, 15. [Icel. maðra.] v. feld-mædere.
mædere-cíþ, es; m. A sprig of madder, Lchdm. i. 397, 2.
m&aelig-acute;d-land, es; m. Meadow-land, grass-land which is mown :-- &AElig-acute;gðer ge m&aelig-acute;dlondes ge eyrþlondes both of land for mowing and of arable land, Cod. Dipl. Kmbl. ii. 95, 16. Médlandes, vi. 219, 4. v. m&aelig-acute;dwe-land.
m&aelig-acute;d-m&aelig-acute;wect, the mowing of a meadow :-- Eác hé sceal hwíltídum geara beón on manegum weorcum tó hláfordes willan tóeácan . . . m&aelig-acute;dm&aelig-acute;wecte also he shall at times be ready for labour of many kinds at his lord's pleasure, besides . . . mowing his meadows, L. R. S. 5; Th. i. 436, 3-5.
m&aelig-acute;d-r&aelig-acute;denn, e; f. A mowing, grass mown on a piece of land :-- Seó m&aelig-acute;dr&aelig-acute;den beniþan díc betweónan cealdan lace and cullig, Cod. Dipl. Kmbl. vi. 153, 10. Cf. wudu-r&aelig-acute;denn.
m&aelig-acute;d-splott, es; m. A plot of meadow-land :-- &AElig-acute;nne m&aelig-acute;dsplot, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iv. 72, 7.
m&aelig-acute;dwa. v. m&aelig-acute;d.
m&aelig-acute;dwe-land, es; n. Meadow-land, land where grass that is to be mown grows :-- Hió sellaþ him ðæt médweland bí westan Sæferne . . Éc twelf æceras gódes m&aelig-acute;dwelandes, Cod. Dipl. Kmbl. ii. 150, 10-18 : vi. 219, 3. v. m&aelig-acute;d-land.
M&AElig-acute;G, es; m. A relative, kinsman :-- M&aelig-acute;g propinquus, Wrt. Voc. 72, 45 : Ælfc. Gr. 5; Som. 4, 51. Hwylc þyncþ ðé ðæt sý ðæs m&aelig-acute;g ðe on ða sceaðan befeóll quis videtur tibi proximus fuisse illi qui incidet in latrones? Lk. Skt. 10, 36. Meig contribulius, Wrt. Voc. ii. 104, 26. Meeg, Ep. Gl. 6 f, 17. Se wæs his m&aelig-acute;g and his freónd and hæfde his sweoster tó wífe qui erat cognatus et amicus ejus, habens sororem ipsius conjugem, Bd. 3, 21; S. 551, 6 : Blickl. Homl. 113, 22. Him cýþdon ðæt hiera m&aelig-acute;gas him mid w&aelig-acute;ron . . And ðá cu&aelig-acute;don hié ðæt him n&aelig-acute;nig m&aelig-acute;g leófra n&aelig-acute;re ðonne hiera hláford . . and ðá budon hié hiera m&aelig-acute;gum ðæt hié gesunde from eodon, Chr. 755; Erl. 50, 17-21. Hér Æþelherd cining forþférde and f&aelig-acute;ng Cúðréd his m&aelig-acute;g tó West-Seaxna ríce, 740; Erl. 47, 33 : 754; Erl. 49, 18 : 962; Erl. 120, 2. Abrahames m&aelig-acute;g (Lot), Cd. 94; Th. 121, 19; Gen. 2012. Higeláces m&aelig-acute;g (Beowulf), Beo. Th. 820; B. 408. Úre ieldesta m&aelig-acute;g our first parent, Past. 43, 5; Swt. 313, 15. Ne h&aelig-acute;me nán man wið his m&aelig-acute;ges (fratris) wíf, Lev. 18, 16. M&aelig-acute;ges filii, Cd. 140; Th. 176, 5; Gen. 2907. Moises heóld his m&aelig-acute;ges (soceri) sceáp, Ex. 3, 1. Moises gecirde tó his m&aelig-acute;ge, 4, 18. Abrahame, m&aelig-acute;ge Lothes, Cd. 141; Th. 177, 2; Gen. 2923. Cénwalh gesalde Cúþréde his m&aelig-acute;ge (fratrueli), Chr. 648; Erl. 26, 15. Ne bysmra ðú ðínne m&aelig-acute;g non facies calumniam proximo tuo, Lev. 19, 13. Gif man gehádodne man oððe ælþeódigne forr&aelig-acute;de ðonne sceal him cyningc beón for m&aelig-acute;g and for mundboran, L. C. S. 40; Th. i. 400, 6. Ne his mágas (fratres) ne gelýfdon on hyne, Jn. Skt. 7, 5. His eorþlícan mágas his kinsmen according to the flesh, Chr. 979; Erl. 129, 12. His mágas and his frýnd cognati atque amici, L. Ecg. C. 36; Th. ii. 160, 22. Gif bana of lande gewíteþ his mágas healfne leód forgelden, L. Ethb. 23; Th. i. 8, 7. Bócland him his m&aelig-acute;gas (MS. B. his yldran) leáfden, L. Alf. pol. 41; Th. i. 88, 16. Hine móton his m&aelig-acute;gas (MS. B. mágas) unsyngian his kindred may exculpate him, L. In. 21; Th. i. 116, 8. Sunu oððe m&aelig-acute;gas (MS. B. mágas), 23; Th. i. 116, 15. Mága affinium, Hpt. Gl. 480, 18. &AElig-acute;nig ðínra mága oððe yldrena aliquis de tuis parentibus aut cognatis, Bd. 2, 12; S. 514, 15. Mid gýmenne mínra mága cura propinquorum, 5, 24; S. 647, 22. Se wæs æðelboren of &aelig-acute;wfæstum mágum he was nobly born of pious parents, Homl. Skt. 4, 3. Suna ic l&aelig-acute;rde ðæt hié hýrdon heora yldrum and heora mágum, Blickl. Homl. 185, 21. Súþ-Seaxe and Eást-Seaxe from his m&aelig-acute;gum (ancestors) &aelig-acute;r mid unryhte ánídde w&aelig-acute;run, Chr. 823; Erl. 62, 23. Gé beóþ gesealde fram mágum and gebróðrum and cúðum and freóndum trademini a parentibus et fratribus et cognatis et amicis, Lk. Skt. 21, 16. L&aelig-acute;raþ eówre suna and eówre mágas docebis filios ac nepotes tuos, Deut. 4, 9. Mágos propinquos, Kent. Gl. 368. Bearn árísaþ ongén mágas insurgent filii in parentes, Mt. Kmbl. 10, 21. Ymbe míne mágas ic hogige erga propinquos curo, Ælfc. Gr. 47; Som. 47, 29. Ðíne leófostan frýnd fæder and módor and ðíne mágas patrem tuum et matrem et omnem cognationem tuam, Jos. 2, s8: Ps. Th. 73, 8. Ealle wyrd forsweóp míne mágas, Beo. Th. 5622; B. 2815 : Blickl. Homl. 139, 16. [Laym. mæi a cousin : Goth. mégs a son-in-law : O. Sax. mág a relation : O. Frs méch : Icel. mágr a father-in-law : O. H. Ger. mág cognatus, affinis.] v. cneó-, fæderen-, freó-, friðe-, heáfod-, hleó-, hylde-, leód-, médren-, neáh-, wine-, woruld-m&aelig-acute;g; un-m&aelig-acute;g; ge-mágas.
m&aelig-acute;g, e; f. A woman, kinswoman :-- Freólecu m&aelig-acute;g (Eve), Cd. 42; Th. 55, 17; Gen. 895 : (Cain's wife), 50; Th. 64, 21; Gen. 1053 : (Hagar), 101; Th. 134, 18; Gen. 2226. Drihtlícu m&aelig-acute;g (Sara), 89; Th. 111, 2; Gen. 1850 : 133; Th. 168, 12; Gen. 2781. M&aelig-acute;g ælfsciéno (Sara), 86; Th. 109, 23; Gen. 1827 : 130; Th. 165, 11; Gen. 2730. Seó eádge m&aelig-acute;g, sancta Maria, Exon. 9 a; Th. 6, 21; Cri. 87. Seó æþele m&aelig-acute;g (Juliana), 68 a; Th. 253, 4; Jul. 175. Seó wuldres m&aelig-acute;g, 74 b; Th. 278, 20; Jul. 600. Cáseres m&aelig-acute;g (Elene), Elen. Kmbl. 660; El. 330 : 1335; El. 669. [Laym. may : Orm. ma&yogh;&yogh; : Chauc. mai.] v. eád-, wyn-m&aelig-acute;g.
mæg may. v. magan.
m&aelig-acute;g-bana, an; m. A destroyer of one's kinsmen :-- Hit (surfeiting) biþ m&aelig-acute;gbana, and hit ne murneþ for nánum men, ne for fæder ne for méder ne for bróðer ne for swuster ne for nánum gesibban men, Wulfst. 242, 5.
m&aelig-acute;g-bót, e; f. The 'bót' paid to the kinsman of a slain man for the slaying of the latter. It seems to be used only in the case of the spiritual relationship of godfather and godchild :-- Gif hwá óðres godsunu sleá oððe his godfæder síe sió m&aelig-acute;gbót and sió manbót gelíc. Weaxe sió bót be ðam were swá ilce swá sió manbót déþ ðe ðam hláforde sceal . . . Gif hé on ðone geonbyrde ðe hine slóg ðonne ætfealle sió bót ðæm godfæder swá ilce swá ðæt wíte ðam hláforde déþ if any one slay another's godson or his godfather, let the compensation to the godfather or godson and that to the lord of the dead man be alike. Let them both increase in proportion to the 'wer' . . . If he (the slain man) strove against him that slew him, then let there be no 'bót' to the godfather just as there is no 'wite' to the lord, L. In. 76; Th. i. 150, 13-20. &AElig-acute;gðer ge m&aelig-acute;gbóte ge manbóte fullíce gebéte, L. C. E. 2; Th. i. 360, 7.
m&aelig-acute;g-burh; gen. -barge; f. Kindred, family, relatives, tribe :-- M&aelig-acute;g-burg cognatio, Wrt. Voc. ii. 15, 70. Weóx under wolcnum m&aelig-acute;gburh Semes, Cd. 82; Th. 102, 20; Gen. 1703 : 100; Th. 132, 14; Gen. 2193 : 81; Th. 102, 4; Gen. 1695. Ne weorþeþ sió m&aelig-acute;gburg gemicledu eaforan mínum, Exon. 105 b; Th. 401, 31; Rä. 21, 20. Heó ongan his m&aelig-acute;gburge men geícean sunum and dóhtrum, Cd. 56; Th. 69, 7; Gen. 1132 : 101; Th. 134, 5; Gen. 2220 : Beo. Th. 5766; B. 2887. Hé hit ne móste sellan of his m&aelig-acute;gburge he might not sell it (bócland) out of the family, L. Alf. pol. 41; Th. i. 88, 18. Wes m&aelig-acute;gburge mínre árfæst be kind to my kindred, Cd. 136; Th. 171, 8; Gen. 2825 : Exon. 88 a; Th. 331, 3; Vy. 62. Gielden siððan his m&aelig-acute;gas ðone wer gif hé m&aelig-acute;gburg (-borh, MS. B.: -burh, MS. H.) hæbbe freó let his kinsmen afterwards pay the wergild, if he have free kindred, L. In. 74; Th. i. 148, 19. M&aelig-acute;gburge míne my children, Exon. 104 b; Th. 397, 15; Rä. 16, 20. Iécte m&aelig-acute;gburg síne, Cd. 55; Th. 68, 27; Gen. 1123. M&aelig-acute;gburh, 52; Th. 65, 14; Gen. 1066. Cúðe &aelig-acute;ghwilc m&aelig-acute;gburga riht each one knew the rights of the tribes, 161; Th. 200, 5; Exod. 352. Ða ðe m&aelig-acute;gburge m&aelig-acute;st gefrunon frumcyn feora fæderæþelo gehwæs those who were best informed as to families, as to the origin of men, and the ancestry of each, Th. 200, 21; Exod. 360.
m&aelig-acute;g-cild, es; n. A young kinsman :-- Hine áhsode hw&aelig-acute;r hé his m&aelig-acute;gcildum cumen hæfde ðe hé him forstolen hæfde asked him what he had done with his young kinsmen (cousins) whom he had stolen away from him, Lchdm. iii. 424, 37. Ðý læs &aelig-acute;nig man cweðe ðæt ic míne m&aelig-acute;gcild mid wó fordémde lest any man say that I wrongfully decided against my kinsmen (nephews), Chart. Th. 486, 27.
m&aelig-acute;g-cúð; adj. Related :-- M&aelig-acute;gcúðre sibbe cognate propinquitatis, Wrt. Voc. ii. 133, 34.
m&aelig-acute;g-cwealm, es; m. Murder of a father or kinsman :-- Mégcualm parricidio, Wrt. Voc. ii. 116, 53.
M&AElig-acute;G-CYNREN -- MÆGEN-EÁCEN. 655
m&aelig-acute;g-cynren, es; n. Race, family:-- Macynnere [= (?) mægcynrene] prosapia, Hpt. Gl. 437, 11.
mægden, mæden, es; n. A maiden, girl, virgin:-- M&aelig-acute;den cíðe geong wífman puella, Wrt. Voc. 73, 5. Nis ðis m&aelig-acute;den ná dead ac heó sl&aelig-acute;pþ. . . Hé nam ðæs m&aelig-acute;denes módor, Mk. Skt. 5, 39-40. Ðú nú sceáwa ðínes mæg(d)enes (the Virgin Mary) eáþmódnesse, Blickl. Homl. 159, 4. Ðá wearþ ðæs mægdnes mód miclum geblissad, Exon. 74b; Th. 279, 3; Jul. 608. Hit sealde ðam m&aelig-acute;dene (the daughter of Herodias), and ðæt m&aelig-acute;den hit sealde hire méder, Mk. Skt. 6, 28. Gif hwá m&aelig-acute;den nýdn&aelig-acute;me si quis violenter virginem opprimat, L. C. S. 53; Th. i. 406, 3. Ne nýde man náðer ne wíf ne m&aelig-acute;den tó ðam ðe hyre sylfre mislícige let no woman, whether she have been married before or not, be forced to a marriage which she dislikes, 75; Th. i. 416, 20: L. Edm. B. 1; Th. i. 254, 2. M&aelig-acute;denu virgines, Ps. Th. 44. 15. Tó abbudissan gehádod ofer má ðonne twám hund m&aelig-acute;denum. Homl. Th. ii. 476, 20. M&aelig-acute;denu niman on þeáwe gódne tíman getácnaþ, Lchdm. iii. 208, 28. [O. H. Ger. magatín: M. H. Ger. magetín.]
mægden-&aelig-acute;w, e; f. Marriage with a virgin:-- Ðæt biþ rihtlíc líf ðæt cniht þurhwunige on his cnihtháde óþ ðæt hé on rihtre m&aelig-acute;den&aelig-acute;we gewífige and hæbbe ða syððan and n&aelig-acute;nige ððre ða hwíle ðe seó libbe that is right life, that a young man remain a bachelor until in lawful matrimony he take a maiden to wife, and let him have her afterwards and no other while she lives, L. I. P. 22; Th. i. 332, 29.
ægden-cild, es; n. A female child, girl:-- Gif hit hysecild byþ ofsleáþ ðæt gif hit sí m&aelig-acute;dencild healdaþ ðæt si masculus fuerit, interficite eum, si femina reservate, Ex. 1, 16. Ðonne ða wíf heora bearn cendon, ðonne féddon hié ða m&aelig-acute;dencild and slógon ða hysecild, and ð&aelig-acute;m m&aelig-acute;dencildum hié fortendun ðæt swíðre breóst foran, Ors. 1, 10; Swt. 46, 10-12. T&aelig-acute;cende ðám m&aelig-acute;dencildum docendo puellas, Ælfc. Gr. 26; Som. 28, 16.
mægden-hád. es; m. Maidenhood, virginity:-- Ðeáh wæs hyre (the Virgin Mary) mægdenhád &aelig-acute;ghwæs onwalg, Exon. 28 b; Th. 87, 5; Cri. 1420. Gif &aelig-acute;nig wer oððe wíf geháte ðæt hé wylle m&aelig-acute;denhád gehealdan si quis vir aui mulier voverit virginitatem servare, L. Ecg. C. 19; Th. ii. 146, 1. v. mægþ-hád.
mægden, m&aelig-acute;den-heáp, es; m. A virgin band, troop of maidens, Dóm. L. 18, 288.
mægden-líc; adj. Maidenly, girlish, virgin, virginal:-- M&aelig-acute;denlíc puellaris, virginalis, Ælfc. Gr. 5; Som. 5, 23. Seó m&aelig-acute;denlice cl&aelig-acute;nnys virginalis castitas, Hymn. Surt. 118, 21. M&aelig-acute;denlícere virginalis, Hpt. Gl. 506, 38. Godes sunu þurh m&aelig-acute;denlícne innoþ ácenned wearþ, Homl. Th. i. 458, 33.
mægden-mann, es; m. A maid, virgin:-- M&aelig-acute;denman virgo. Wrt. Voc. 73, 6. Gá án m&aelig-acute;denman to, and hó hit on his sweoran, Lchdm. iii. 42, 9. Gif hwylc m&aelig-acute;denman on geférr&aelig-acute;dene mid gehádodum wunaþ si puella aliqua in societate cum ordinatis habitet, L. Ecg. P. ii. 17; Th. ii. 188, 9. Gif man wið cyninges mægdenman geligeþ, L. Ethb. 10; Th. i. 6, 4. Forðon Mesiane noldon ðæt Læcedemonia mægdenmenn mid heora ofreden and heora godum onsægden propter spretas virgines suas in solemni Messeniorum sacrificio, Ors. 1, 14; Swt. 56, 16. [Orm. Sannte Mar&yogh;e wass æfre ma&yogh;&yogh;dennmann.] v. mægt-mann.
m&aelig-acute;ge, an; f. A kinswoman:-- Elizabeth ðín m&aelig-acute;ge (MSS. A. B. mage. ) Elisabeth cognata tua. Lk. Skt. 1. 36. Hér sit Leófl&aelig-acute;d mín m&aelig-acute;ge, Ðurcilles wíf, Chart. Th. 337, 30. Cwæð ðæt heó w&aelig-acute;re gramena m&aelig-acute;ge, Deáðes dóhtor, Homl. Skt. 2. 173. Saga ðæt ðú síe sweostor mín, líces m&aelig-acute;ge, Cd. 89; Th. 110, 4; 6611. 1833: 127; Th. 162, 18; Gen. 2683. In Dauides dýrre m&aelig-acute;gan (the Virgin Mary), Exon. 9a; Th. 7, 5; Cri. 96. v. máge, m&aelig-acute;g.
Mægelan, Mægelang, Milan:-- Tó Mægelan [Mægolange, MS. C.] apud Mediolanum, Ors. 6, 36; Swt. 294, 30.
MÆGEN, T. es; n. I. MAIN, might, strength, force, power, vigour, efficacy, virtue, faculty, ability:-- Úrum líchoman cymþ eall his mægen of ðam mete ðe wé þicgaþ all its strength comes to our body from the food that we take, Bt. 34, 11; Fox 150, 34. Ðæt mycle mægen mínra handa the mighty power of my hands. Ps. Th. 80, 13. Micel drihten úre and micel mægen his Magnus Dominus noster, et magna virtus ejus, Ps. Spl. 146, 5. Ð&aelig-acute;m monnum ðe him mægen and cræft wiexþ eác hwílum eákiaþ æfter ðæm mægenum ða costunga crescente virtute plerumque bella tentationis augentur, Past. 21, 5; Swt. 163, 8. Se wæs moncynnes mægenes strengest he was mightiest among men, Beo. Th. 395; B. 196. Nánne man ðæs ne tweóþ ðæt se seó strong on his mægene ðe mon gesihþ ðæt stronglíc weorc wyrcþ nemo dubitat esse fortem, cui fortitudinem inesse conspexerit, Bt. 16, 3; Fox 54, 28. &AElig-acute;r hí geseón Godes ríce on mægne cuman donec videant regnum dei veniens in virtute, Mk. Skt. 9, 1. Hé sealde &aelig-acute;ghwylcum be hys ágenum mægene dedit unicuique secundum propriam virlutem, Mt. Kmbl. 25, 15. Lufa ðínne drihten mid eallum mægne diliges dominum tuum ex tota forlitudine tua, Deut. 6, 5. Of eallum ðínum mihtum and of eallum ðínum mægene ex omnibus viribus tuis et ex omni mente tua, Lk. Skt. 10, 27. Eallon mægene tilian, Bt. 24, 2 ; Fox 82, 6. Wiðstandan ealle mægene, Past. 15, 1; Swt. 91, 1: Beo. Th. 5328; B. 2667. Ðú ne wénst ðæt heó m&aelig-acute;ge swá mycel mægen habban you will not expect that the plant. can have so great efficacy. Herb. 12, 4; Lchdm. i. 104, 12. Hé moncynnes m&aelig-acute;ste hæfde mægen and strengo, Cd. 79; Th. 98, 19; Gen. 1632. Ða ðe snyttro mægn and módcræft m&aelig-acute;ste hæbben those who in the greatest degree have wisdom, ability and menial power, Elen. Kmbl. 815; El. 408. Ðonne hí ðæt mægen ðære unm&aelig-acute;tan h&aelig-acute;to áræfnan ne mihton cum vim fervoris immensi tolerare non possent, Bd. 5, 12; S. 627, 41. Mægyn and mihta (angeli) poteníes virtute. Ps. Th. 102, 19. Eall his bearna mægen omnes virtutes ejus, 20. Seó sýfernes and óðre mægnu sobrietas et alie virtutes, Prud. 54a: 64a. Ðá sóðan welan ðæt sind hálige mægnu the true riches, they are holy virtues, Homl. Th. ii. 88, 310. Mægenu, Basil admn. 2; Norm. 38, 9. Mægno and cræftas, Bt. 32, 1; Fox 116, 1. Wísdóm módur eallra mægena virtutum omnium nutrix, 10; Fox 26, 24. Mycelre mægna f&aelig-acute;mne magnarum virgo virtutum, Bd. 3, 8; S. 531, 12. Geleáfa is ealra mægena fyrmest, Homl. Th. 1. 134, 2. Geþyld is wyrtruma ealra háligra mægna, and ungeþyld is ealra mægna tóstencednys, ii. 544, 6. Þurh dínra mægna spéd through the abundance of thy powers, Bt. Met. Fox 20, 516; Met. 20, 258: Cd. 1; Th. 1. 6; Gen. 3. Eallum hire mihtum and mægenum, L. M. 3, 63; Lchdm. ii. 352, 5. Ða ðe faraþ fram leahtrum tó mæignum those who pass from vices to virtues, Homl. Th. ii. 54, 26. Mægnum, Prud. 28a. Ða ongunnon hí mód and mægen niman . . . Mód and mægen Bryttas onféngon ceperunt illi vires animosque resumere . . . vires capessunt Brittones, Bd. 1, 16; S. 484, 15-19. Ðeáh ðe ic nú gyt ða &aelig-acute;rran mægen ne hæbbe etsi necdum vires pristinas recepi, 5, 3; S. 616, 34: 5, 4; S. 617, 25. Heó hæfþ ðás mægnu it (henbane) has these virtues, Herb. 5, 1; Lchdm. i. 94, 10. Megene vires, Kent. Gl. 930. II. an exercise of power, effort, a mighty work, miracle:-- Mægene conamine. Wit. Voc. ii. 24, 57. Hé ne mihte &aelig-acute;nig mægen wyrcan non poterat virtutem ullam facere, Mk. Skt. 6, 5. Án mægen and án wundor of monegum ásecgan unum e pluribus virtutis miraculum enarrare, Bd. 3, 2; S. 524, 38. Monige mægen and h&aelig-acute;lotácen gefremede w&aelig-acute;ron innumeræ virtutes sanitatum noscuntur esse patratæ, S. 524, 28. On him synd mægenu geworht, Mk. Skt. 6, 14. Ða burga on ðám w&aelig-acute;run gedóne manega hys mægena, Mt. Kembl. 11, 20. III. a force, military force:-- Gif ðet full mægen ð&aelig-acute;re w&aelig-acute;re ne eodan hí n&aelig-acute;fre eft tó scipon if the full force had been there, they would never have got back to the ships, Chr. 1004; Erl. 139, 34. Úre mægen lytlaþ our force lessens. Byrht. Th. 140, 65; By. 313. Mægen, folc Ebréa, Judth. 12; Thw. 25, 15, 10; Jud. 261, 253. Werod, módigra mægen, Cd. 147; Th. 184, 2; Exod. 101: 158; Th. 197, 1; Exod. 300. Mægen forþgewát, 160; Th. 199, 30; Exod. 346. Mægen (the Egyptian army) wæs ádrenced, 166; Th. 206, 28; Exod. 458. Seó sibgedriht bád máran mægenes the Israelites awaited the greater force of the Egyptians, 154; Th. 191, 15; Exod. 215. Mægenes wísa (Belshazzar), 209; Th. 260, 2; Dan. 703. Se wæs mid his d&aelig-acute;dum snelra ðonne hé mæ[ge]nes hæfde he was quicker in his actions than in proportion to the force he had; celeritate magis quam virtute fretus, Ors. 2, 5; Swt. 78, 27. Hé self fór ð&aelig-acute;rtó mid eallum ðæm mægene ðe hé ð&aelig-acute;rtó gel&aelig-acute;dan mehte he himself marched thither with all the troops that he could lead there, Swt. 80, 24. Martyra mægen unlytel no small host of martyrs, Andr. Kmbl. 1752; An. 878: Beo. Th. 894; B. 445. Mægen unríme hosts innumerable, Elen. Kmbl. 121; El. 61. [O. Sax. megin: Icel. magn and megin: O. H. Ger. magan, megin, robur, vigor, vis, virtus, fortitudo.] DER. beadu-, deáþ-, eal-(æl-), eorþ-, eorl-, folc-, gæst-, gesíþ-, hand-, here-, heáh-, heofon-, holm-, hord-, leód-, lof-, ofer-, r&aelig-acute;d-, tóþ-, þeód-mægen.
mægen-ágende; adj. Possessing strength, mighty, Beo. Th. 5666; B. 2837.
mægen-byrðtenn, e; f. A mighty burden, Beo. Th. 3254; B. 1625: 6174; B. 3091.
mregen-corþer, es; n. A powerful band, Cd. 93; Th. 119, 27; Gen. 1986.
mægen-cræft, es; m. Main force, great power or might, mighty power: -- Mægencræft ðe him meotud engla forgiefen hæfde the power which the Lord of angels had given him, Exon. 49 a; Th. 170, I; Gú. 1105. Is ðæt mægencræft micel móda gehwylces ofer líchoman (cf. hit is micel cræft ðæs módes for ðone líchoman, Bt. 38, 1; Fox 196, 10), Bt. Met. Fox 26, 209; Met. 26, 105. Ðæt he þrittiges manna mægencræft on his mundgripe hæbbe, Beo. Th. 765; B. 380. Mircne mægencræft, Exon. 26b; Th. 78, 26; Cri. 1280. [O. Sax. megin-kraft: O. L. Ger. megin-craft majestas: O. H. Ger. magan-kraft majestas.]
mægen-cyning, es; m. A chief, mighty or powerful king:-- Mægencyning (God), Elen. Kmbl. 2493; El. 1248: Exon. 116b; Th. 448, 21; Dóm. 57: (Christ), 21a; Th. 57, 11; Cri. 917. Mægencyninga meotod the lord of mighty kings, 21b; Th. 58, 29; Cri. 943: 116a; Th. 445, 12; Dóm. 6. [Cf. Icel. megin-dróttning (the Virgin Mary): megin-skjöldungr (Christ).]
mægen-d&aelig-acute;d, e; f. A mighty deed, an action requiring strength, Exon. 78b; Th. 294, 9; Crä 12.
mægen-eáca, an; m. An increase of strength, succour:-- Monnum tó mægeneácan a succour for men. Exon. 55a; Th. 194, 14; Az. 138.
mægen-eácen; adj. Endowed with strength, powerful:-- Móde macgen-
656 MÆGEN-EARFEÞE--MÆG-HAND.
eácen, Exon. 79 b; Th. 299, 7; Crä. 98. Mægeneácen folc (the victorious Hebrews), Judth. 12; Thw. 25, 35; Jud. 293.
mægen-earfeþe, es; n. A great labour or hardship:--Nales fore lytlum geómre, ac fore ðám m&aelig-acute;stum mægenearfeþum, Exon. 22 a; Th. 60, 4; Cri. 964. Mægenearfeþu, sár and swár gewin and sweartne deáþ, 28b; Th. 86, 20; Cri. 1411.
mægen-ellen, es; n. Mighty valour, Beo. Th. 1323; B. 659.
mægen-fæst, adj. Strong, vigorous, firm:--Sealde him snyttru mægenfæste gemynd he gave him wisdom, vigorous thought, Exon. 39 b; Th. 130, 28; Gú. 445. &AElig-acute;lc líchamlíce gesceaft ðe eorþe ácenþ is fulre and mægenfæstre on fullum mónan ðonne on gewanedum every bodily creature that earth produces is more complete and more vigorous at the full moon than when the moon has waned, Homl. Th. i. 102, 21. [Cf. mægen-leás.]
mægen-folc, es; n. A mighty people:--Mægenfolc micel (cf. O. Sax. meginfolk mikil the multitude that flocked about Christ) a people mighty and vast (the good at the day of judgment), Exon. 20 b; Th. 55, 1; Cri. 877.
mægen-fultum, es; m. A powerful help:--Næs ðæt m&aelig-acute;tost mægenfultuma (the sword lent to Beowulf by Hunferth), Beo. Th. 2915; B. 1455.
mægen-heáp, es; m. A powerful band:--Mægenheápum, Cd. 151; Th. 190, 11; Exod. 197.
mægen-heard; adj. Very strong, powerful:--Ðam ðe sitteþ on ufan meare mægenheardum, Runic pm. 5; Kmbl. 340, 5.
mægenian, mægnian; p. ode To gain strength:--Mód mægnode mind gained might, Exon. 94 b; Th. 353, 55; Reim. 33. v. ge-mægened.
mægen-leás; adj. Without strength, powerless, weak, feeble:--Mægenleás enervis, Wrt. Voc. i. 46, 6: elumbis, Germ. 396, 216. Seó sáwul, gif heó næfþ ða hálgan láre, heó biþ ðonne weornigende and mægenleás, Homl. Th. i. 168, 33. Icel. megin-lauss.]
mægenleas-líce; adv. Feebly, impotently:--Mægenleaslíce eviscerando, Germ. 398, 122.
mægen-leást, e; f. Weakness, feebleness, impotence:--Ðá ofhreów ðam munece ðæs hreóflian mægenleást (inability to walk), Homl. Th. i. 336, 11. Módes mægenleást weakness of mind, ii. 220, 5. Hí ne mihton for heora mægenleáste ða meniu bewerian (of the Jews reduced by famine during the siege of Jerusalem), Ælfc. T. Grn. 21, 8.
mægen-r&aelig-acute;s, es; m. A mighty or violent attack:--Mægenr&aelig-acute;s forgeaf hilde bille (Beowulf attacking Grendel's mother), Beo. Th. 3043; B. 1519.
mægen-róf; adj. Of great power:--Módig and mægenróf mid ðære miclan hand (applied to God), Cd. 156; Th. 195, 11; Exod. 275. Þegn, mægenrófa man, Exon. 109 b; Th. 419, 9; Rä. 38, 3.
mægen-scipe, es; m. Power, might:--Metodes mægenscipe, Cd. 173; Th. 217, 9; Dan. 20.
mægen-spéd, e; f. Abundance of strength, strength (cf. on ðínes mægenes miclum spédum in virtute tua, Ps. Th. 73, 13), power, virtue:--Ic ðé sceal meotudes mægenspéd gesecgan to thee am I to tell the Maker's abundant might, Exon. 92 b; Th. 348, 6; Sch. 24. Hé mec for miltsum and mægenspédum n&aelig-acute;fre wille án forl&aelig-acute;tan on account of his mercy and his might he will never forsake me, 42 a; Th. 140, 17; Gú. 611: Andr. Kmbl. 2572; An. 1287. Mín múþ sægeþ ðíne mægenspéde os meum pronuntiabit justitiam tuam, Ps. Th. 70, 14.
mægen-stán, es; m. A mighty stone or rock:--Him on innan felþ muntes mægenstán (cf. þ&aelig-acute;r micel stán wealwiende of ðam heáhan munte on innan fealþ, Bt. 6; Fox 14, 28), Bt. Met. Fox 5, 31; Met. 5, 16. Ðis synd ðæra xx hída gem&aelig-acute;ro . . andlang wægæs óþ ðonæ mægenstán, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. v. 112, 18.
mægen-strang; adj. Strong in power:--Hú ðú m&aelig-acute;re eart mihtig and mægenstrang how great thou (Christ) art, how mighty and strong in power, Hy. 3, 21; Hy. Grn. ii. 282, 21. Ðú eart se miccla and se mægenstranga, 3, 38; Hy. Grn. ii. 282, 38. Mægenstrong, Exon. 129 a; Th. 495. 5; Rä. 84, 3.
mægen-strengo; indecl. f. Main strength, great force:--Gúþcyning (Beowulf) mægenstrengo slóh hilde bille with mighty force the warrior-king smote with his battle-blade, Beo. Th. 5350; B. 2678. Sum biþ gleáw módes cræfta sum mægenstrengo onféhþ one is skilled in the arts of the mind, another receives great bodily strength, Exon. 78 b; Th. 295, 15; Crä. 33.
mægen-strengþu; indecl.: -strengþ, e; f. Great strength, power:--Hí ðíne mægenstrengþu m&aelig-acute;rsien wíde magnitudinem tuam narrabunt, Ps. Th. 144, 6. Ic siges mihte and mægenstrengþe swá micele eów sille ðæt gé eów tó gamene feónda áfillaþ swá fela swá gé reccaþ I will give you so great victorious might and power, that it shall be sport to you to slay as many foes as you can count, Wulfst. 132, 19.
mægen-þegen, es; m. A mighty minister (an angel), Exon. 49 a; Th. 169, 23; Gú. 1099.
mægen-þreát, es; m. A mighty band, Cd. 174; Th. 218, 26; Dan. 45: 169; Th. 210, 8; Exod. 512.
mægen-þrymm, es; m. (The word is used almost exclusively in reference to the Deity). I. Majesty, greatness, glory:--Se myccla mægenþrym the great majesty (of Christ), Blickl. Homl. 179, 8. Mægenþrymmes God Deus majestatis, Ps. Th. 28, 3. Mægenþrymmes ðínes majestatis tuæ, 144, 5. His mægenþrymmes magnitudinis ejus, 150, 2. His ríces ongin, ne his mihte, ne his mægenþrymmes n&aelig-acute;fre gewonad ne weorþeþ, Blickl. Homl. 9, 17. Hé (Christ) hine ungyrede ðæs godcundan mægenþrymmes, and gegyrede hine þeówlíce, 105, 3. Ðonne se heofenlíca déma cymþ on egeslícum mægenþrymme, Homl. Th. ii. 558, 9: Lk. Skt. 9, 26, 31, 32. Mid ðý m&aelig-acute;stan mægenþrymme, Exon. 22 b; Th. 62, 30: Cri. 1009. Johannes on Godes mægenþrymme hí gebletsode, Homl. Th. i. 64, 4. Wé gesáwon Godes mægenþrim and his micelnisse (majestatem et magnitudinem suam), Deut. 5, 24. II. (using the attribute for the person), Christ:--Mægenþrym árás, sigefæst and snottor, Exon. 120 a; Th. 420, 25; Hö. 22. III. great power, might:--Gé geseóþ mannes Bearn sittende on ða swýðran healfe Godes mægenþrymmes videbitis filium hominis sedentem a dextris virtutis Dei, Mt. Kmbl. 26, 64. Ic sóhte hwylc w&aelig-acute;re mægenþrymmes oððe elnes se Pater Noster, Salm. Kmbl. 20; Sal. 10. In ðam mægenþrymme mid ðam sý áhefed heofon and eorþe in that mighty power with which is uplifted heaven and earth, Exon. 93 b; Th. 351, 31; Sch. 88. Hé hine of sáwle deáþe áwehte þurh ðone mægenþrym he raised him from the death of the soul through divine power, Blickl. Homl. 77, 10. Mægenþrymmum m&aelig-acute;st mightiest, Cd. 160; Th. 199, 35; Exod. 349. IV. an instance in which the divine glory or power is displayed:--Eftwyrd cymþ, mægenþrymma m&aelig-acute;st, dæg d&aelig-acute;dum fáh (doom's day), Cd. 169; Th. 212, 16; Exod. 540. V. the glory of heaven, heaven, the angels who inhabit heaven:--Wuldres ealdor middangeardes and mægenþrymmes the prince of glory, of earth and of heaven, Exon. 68 a; Th. 251, 33; Jul. 154. Hé is cyning middangeardes and mægenþrymmes, wuldre biwunden, 65 b; Th. 241, 33; Ph. 665: 16 a; Th. 35, 13; Cri. 557. Ufan of roderum, of his mægenþrymme, 98 a; Th. 368, 24; Seel. 29. Héht sigores fruma his heáhbodan hider (to earth) gefleógan of his mægenþrymme, 12 a; Th. 19, 5; Cri. 296. Næs &aelig-acute;nig ðá giet engel geworden ne ðæs miclan mægenþrymmes nán was not any angel then created, nor any of that great and glorious band, 12 b; Th. 22, 16; Cri. 352.
mægenþrym-ness, e; f. Majesty, magnificence, glory:--His mægenþrymnes (-þrymmes, MS.) micellíc standeþ magnificentia opus ejus, Ps. Th. 110, 2. Mæg[en]þrymnysse majestatis, Hpt. Gl. 486, 18. Ælmihtig God, ánes gecyndes, and ánre mægenþrymnisse on ánre godcundnysse, Hexam. 2; Norm. 4, 23. Ðonne sit hé on dómsetle his mægenþrymnysse, Wulfst. 287, 31. Mæg[n]þrumnysse majestati, Hpt. Gl. 416, 52. God sylf se ðe &aelig-acute;fre þurhwunode on his miclan wuldre and on his mægenþrimnisse, Ælfc. T. Grn. 2, 4. Ða ðe gesáwon míne mægenþrimnisse qui viderunt majestatem meam, Num. 14, 22.
mægen-þyse, an; f. Violence, force:--Sóna ðæt onfindeþ se ðe mec féhþ ongeán and wið mægenþisan mínre gen&aelig-acute;steþ ðæt hé hrycge sceal hrusan sécan soon doth he find that fights against me, and with my force comes into conflict, that with his back he must visit the earth, Exon. 107 b; Th. 410, 2; Rä. 28, 10. [Cf. Icel. þysja to rush.]
mægen-weorc, es; n. A mighty work:--Hú micle synt ðíne mægenweorc quam magnificata sunt opera tua, Ps. Th. 91, 4. [Icel. megin-verk; pl. mighty works.]
mægen-wísa, an; m. The leader of a force or army, Cd. 170; Th. 213, 17; Exod. 553.
mægen-wudu, a.; m. A mighty spear-shaft:--þegn Hróðgáres cwehte mægenwudu mundum Hrothgar's thane shook his mighty shaft with his hands, Beo. Th. 477; B. 236.
mægen-wundor, es; n. A very great wonder (of the circumstances attending the day of judgement), Exon. 21 b; Th. 57, 31; Cri. 927.
mæger; adj. Meagre, lean:--Ða men beóþ mægre and bláce on onsýne ðeáh ðe hié &aelig-acute;r fætte w&aelig-acute;ron the men will be lean and pale of aspect, though before they were fat, L. M. 2, 36; Lchdm. ii. 242, 3. [Icel. magr: Dan., Swed., Du. mager: O. H. Ger. magar macilentus: Ger. mager.]
mægerian; p. ode To macerate, emaciate, make lean:--Mægeregan macerare, Wrt. Voc. ii. 57, 16: 96, 34. [Icel. megra to emaciate: O. H. Ger. magarian macerare, macrescere; cf. magar fleiski pulpa: Ger. magern.]
mægeþ, m&aelig-acute;geþ. v. mægþ, m&aelig-acute;gþ.
mægeþe name of a plant. v. mageþe.
m&aelig-acute;g-gemót, es; n. A meeting of kinsmen:--Hé bebeád ofer ealne middangeard ðæt &aelig-acute;lc m&aelig-acute;gþ tógædere cóme, ðæt &aelig-acute;lc man ðý gearor wiste hw&aelig-acute;r hé gesibbe hæfde. Ðæt tácnode ðæt on his dagum sceolde beón geboren se se ðe ús ealle tó ánum m&aelig-acute;ggemóte gelaþaþ, Ors. 5, 14; Swt. 248, 18.
m&aelig-acute;g-gewrit, es; n. A writing containing a list of kinsmen, a genealogical table, pedigree, Cot. 213, Lye.
méég-gildan (?) to pay part of the wergild for a homicide committed by a kinsman:--Ne þearf se frigea mid ðam þeówan m&aelig-acute;ggieldan (or should this be m&aelig-acute;ge gieldan? cf. MS. B. which has mid ðam þeówan men gyldan. But the word is supported by L. H. i. 70, 5:--Non cogitur liber cum servo meggildare), L. In. 74; Th. i. 150, 1.
m&aelig-acute;g-h&aelig-acute;med, es; n. Incest:--N&aelig-acute;nig m&aelig-acute;gh&aelig-acute;med ne uncl&aelig-acute;ne fremme nullus incestum faciat, Bd. 4, 5; S. 573, 15.
m&aelig-acute;g-hand, a; f. A relation, kinsman:--Nis Eðelmóde énig méghond
MÆGISTER--M&AElig-acute;GÞ, M&AElig-acute;GEÞ. 657
neór ðes cynnes ðanne Eádwald there is no nearer relative to Ethelmod in the family than Eadwald, Chart. Th. 466, 1. Wes hit becueden his bróðar suna and siððan néniggra méihanda má ðes cynnes, 465, 20. Cf. ða nýhstan hand mé, 491, 13.
mægister. v. magister.
m&aelig-acute;g-lagu, e; f. Law regulating the duties and responsibilities of kinsmen (m&aelig-acute;gas), e. g. in the matter of paying or receiving certain parts of the wergild if one of their number slew or was slain:--Hé (mynster-munuc) g&aelig-acute;þ of his m&aelig-acute;glage ðonne hé gebýhþ tó regollage, L. Eth. ix. 25; Th. i. 346, 2. v. m&aelig-acute;gþ-lagu and lagu.
m&aelig-acute;g-leás; adj. Without kinsmen:--Gif hé sí m&aelig-acute;gleás if he have no kinsmen, L. Eth. ix. 24; Th. i. 344, 28: L. In. 23; Th. i. 116, 16: L. C. E. 5; Th. i. 362, 24. Fædrenm&aelig-acute;ga m&aelig-acute;gleás mon a man having no kinsmen on the father's side, L. Alf. pol. 27; Th. i. 78, 20.
m&aelig-acute;g-líc; adj. Belonging to kinsmen:--Hé hine lufode ná swá micclum for ðære m&aelig-acute;glícan sibbe he loved him, not so much because they were relations, Homl. Th. i. 58, 4. Næfde hé ðæt andgit þurh m&aelig-acute;glíce láre he did not have that intelligence through the teaching of his parents, 368, 10.
m&aelig-acute;g-lufu, an; f. Love:--Heó sagaþ ðæt heó m&aelig-acute;glufan mínre ne gýme she (Juliana) says that she cares not for my (Heliseus', who wished to marry Juliana) love, Exon. 66 b; Th. 246, 31; Jul. 70.
m&aelig-acute;g-morðor, es; n. Murder of a kinsman:--M&aelig-acute;gmorðor parricidium, Hpt. Gl. 519, 74. M&aelig-acute;gmorðres wítnung parricidii actio, Ælfc. Gl. 14; Som. 58, 15; Wrt. Voc. 21, 10. [Cf. O. H. Ger. mág-mord parricidium.]
m&aelig-acute;g-myrðra, an; m. One who murders a kinsman, a parricide:--M&aelig-acute;gmyrðra parricida, Wrt. Voc. ii. 67, 15: Hpt. Gl. 509, 72.
mægn. v. mægen.
m&aelig-acute;g-racu, e; f. The account of a family, a genealogy:--Ðis is seó bóc Adames m&aelig-acute;grace hic est liber generationis Adam, Gen. 5, 1. Gif ðú telst ða m&aelig-acute;grace fram Judan ðonne findst ðú fíf m&aelig-acute;gþa if you reckon the genealogy from Judah, then you will find five generations, Boutr. Scrd. 22, 19.
m&aelig-acute;g-r&aelig-acute;denn, e; f. Kinship, relationship:--Gesibbere m&aelig-acute;gr&aelig-acute;dene consanguinitatis, Hpt. Gl. 472, 20. Hé (Julius Cæsar) hiene (Octavianus) for m&aelig-acute;gr&aelig-acute;denne gel&aelig-acute;rde, Ors. 5, 13; Swt. 244, 24. N&aelig-acute;fre ic ðæs þeódnes þafian wille m&aelig-acute;gr&aelig-acute;denne I will never consent to marry the prince, Exon. 67 a; Th. 249, 9; Jul. 109.
m&aelig-acute;g-r&aelig-acute;s, es; m. An attack by men upon their kinsmen:--Wearþ ðes þeódscype swýðe forsyngod þurh morðd&aelig-acute;da and þurh mánd&aelig-acute;da . . þurh m&aelig-acute;gr&aelig-acute;sas and þurh manslihtas this nation is sunk in sin through deeds fell and foul . . through attacks of kinsmen upon kinsmen and through manslaughters, Wulfst. 164, 4.
m&aelig-acute;g-scír, e; f. A division of a people, containing the kinsmen of a particular family:--Teá monna látwu ofer téno oððe of mégscíre is decanus super x. vel decurio (the glosser seems to have taken de as a separate word) est, Rtl. 193, 19.
m&aelig-acute;g-sibb, e; f. I. kinship, relationship:--Eva hine hálsode for s&c-tilde;a Marian m&aelig-acute;gsibbe ðæt hé hire miltsade. Heó cwæþ tó him gemyne mín drihten ðæt heó wæs bán of mínum bánum and fl&aelig-acute;sc of mínum fl&aelig-acute;sce Eve conjured him (Christ) on account of her kinship to St. Mary to pity her. She said to him 'Remember, my Lord, that she was bone of my bone and flesh of my flesh,' Shrn. 68, 15. Hé (Christ) hym (men) his mildse onwreáh and his m&aelig-acute;gsibbe gecýdde. &AElig-acute;r ðam wé w&aelig-acute;ron steópcild gewordene, Wulfst. 252, 9: Blickl. Homl. 107, 2. Wel is tó warnianne ðæt man wite ðæt hý (the man and woman about to be married) þurh m&aelig-acute;gsibbe tó gelænge ne beón (i. e. are not within the prohibited (seven) degrees), L. Edm. B. 9; Th. i. 256, 9. Seó hálige &aelig-acute; forbeódeþ ða sceondlícnysse onwreón m&aelig-acute;gsibba (ðære m&aelig-acute;gsibbea, MS. B.) sacra lex prohibet cognationis turpitudinem revelare, Bd. 1, 27; S. 491, 7. II. Love between kinsmen, affection:--Mégsibbe affectui vel dilectione, Wrt. Voc. ii. 99, 52. Mégsibbi, Ep. Gl. 3 b, 9.
m&aelig-acute;gsib-líc; adj. Of kin, related:--M&aelig-acute;gsiblícum contribulibus, Wrt. Voc. ii. 20, 18.
m&aelig-acute;g-slaga, an; m. The slayer of a kinsman:--M&aelig-acute;gslaga parricida, Ælfc. Gl. 85; Som. 73, 114; Wrt. Voc. 49, 21: Ælfc. Gr. 7; Som. 6, 46. Se m&aelig-acute;gslaga Cain the fratricide Cain, Homl. Th. ii. 58, 28. Hér syndan mannslagan and m&aelig-acute;gslagan, Wulfst. 165, 27: 266, 26.
m&aelig-acute;g-sliht, es; m. The slaughter of a kinsman:--Wearþ ðes þeódscipe swíðe forsingod þurh manslihtas and þurh m&aelig-acute;gslihtas, Wulfst. 130, 2. [O. H. Ger. mág-slaht; f. parricidium.]
mægþ, mægeþ; without inflection in the sing. and in the n. ac. pl., f. A maid, virgin, girl, maiden, woman (almost confined to poetry):--Gif man mægþ gebigeþ ceápe geceápod sý gif hit unfácne is if a man make terms for his marriage with (lit. buys with a price, cf. Icel. kona mundi keypt) a woman, let the bargain stand, if it be without fraud, L. Ethb. 77; Th. i. 22, 1. Wæs seó f&aelig-acute;mne geong, mægþ mánes leás (the Virgin Mary), Exon. 8 a; Th. 3, 14; Cri. 36. On f&aelig-acute;mnan, mægeþ unm&aelig-acute;le, 18 b; Th. 45, 18; Cri. 721: 122 b; Th. 470, 14; Hy. 11, 16. Þa torhtan mægþ (Judith), Judth. 10; Thw. 22, 1; Jud. 35. Mægþ scýne maiden fair, Beo. Th. 6025; B. 3016. Ofer mægþ giunge, Bt. Met. Fox 26, 134; Met. 26, 67. Þurh Judithe láre, mægþ módigre, Judth. 12; Thw. 26, 18; Jud. 335. Mægeþ, brýde ðínre (Sarah), Cd. 134; Th. 169, 10; Gen. 2797. Hé ðære mægeþ (Guthlac's sister) sceolde láce gel&aelig-acute;dan láð spel, Exon. 52 a; Th. 182, 27; Gú. 1316. Mægþ and mæcgas, 45 a; Th. 153, 29; Gú. 833. Mægeþ and mæcgas, 113 a; Th. 434, 7; Rä. 51, 7. Him tó nimaþ mægeþ tó gemæccum take to themselves maidens as mates, Cd. 64; Th. 76, 18; Gen. 1259. Mægþa síð the maidens' coming, 123; Th. 157, 11; Gen. 2604: Beo. 1853; B. 924. Swá hwylc mægþa swá ðone magan cende, 1890; B. 943. Mægþa cynnes of womankind, Exon. 73 b; Th. 275, 16; Jul. 551. Mægþum and mæcgum, Cd. 55; Th. 68, 26; Gen. 1123. [Goth. magaþs a maid, virgin: O. Sax. magað: O. Frs. megith: O. H. Ger. magad virgo: M. H. Ger. maget: Ger. magd.] v. heals-mægeþ.
m&aelig-acute;gþ, e; f. Importunate desire, ambition:--Ðæt mód s&aelig-acute;de ðæt him n&aelig-acute;fre seó m&aelig-acute;gþ and seó gítsung forwel ne lícode, Bt. tit. 17; Fox xii, 24. Cf. Ðú wást ðæt mé n&aelig-acute;fre seó gítsung and seó gem&aelig-acute;gþ ðisses eorþlícan anwealdes forwel ne lícode scis ipsa minimum nobis ambitionem mortalium rerum fuisse dominatum, 17; Fox 58, 23. v. máh, ge-m&aelig-acute;hþ (with which ge-m&aelig-acute;gþ in the above passage should be put).
m&aelig-acute;gþ, m&aelig-acute;geþ, e; f. A collection of m&aelig-acute;gas. I. with a more limited extent, a family, stock, race:--M&aelig-acute;gþ oððe styb styrps, Ælfc. Gr. 3; Som. 3, 17. M&aelig-acute;gþ progenies, Wrt. Voc. 72, 48: cognatio, Ps. Spl. 73, 9. Mýgþ propinquus, Kent. Gl. 876. Ðá wæs án m&aelig-acute;gþ ðe n&aelig-acute;fre ne ábeáh tó nánum deófolgylde . . Seó m&aelig-acute;gþ ásprang of Noes eltstan suna . . And ðyssere m&aelig-acute;gþe God sealde &aelig-acute; . . forðan ðe hé wolde of ðyssere m&aelig-acute;gþe him módor geceósan, Homl. Th. i. 24, 5-20. Woldon ofsleán Claudius for Gaiuses þingum ðæs &aelig-acute;rran césares and ealle ða de ðære m&aelig-acute;gþe w&aelig-acute;ron evertenda penitus Caesarum universa familia decrevissent, Ors. 6, 4; Swt. 258, 25. Rím miclade monna m&aelig-acute;gþe, Cd. 63; Th. 75, 22; Gen. 1244. M&aelig-acute;gþe ðínre (Abraham's), 84; Th. 105, 34; Gen. 1763. Nis nán wítega búton wurþscipe búton on his éðele and on his m&aelig-acute;gþe (cognatione) and on his húse, Mk. Skt. 6, 4. Ða hwíle ðe &aelig-acute;nig man w&aelig-acute;re on hira m&aelig-acute;gþe ðe godcundes hádes beón walde as long as there was any man of their stock that was willing to take orders, Chart. Th. 166, 16. II. as a technical term in the laws, relatives, kindred, the m&aelig-acute;gas who were living at the same time, and to whom the m&aelig-acute;g-lagu applied:--Gá seó m&aelig-acute;gþ him on borh let the family go bail for him (the thief), L. Ath. i. 1; Th. i. 198, 24. Gif ðonne ðæt gebyrige ðæt &aelig-acute;nig m&aelig-acute;gþ tó ðan strang sý . . ðæt ðonne þeóf foran forstande, V. 8, 2; Th. i. 236, 9: 12, 2; Th. i. 242, 3: L. Edm. S. 1; Th. i. 248, 5. Béte ðam cyninge swá ilce swá ðære m&aelig-acute;gþe let amends be made to the king in the same way as to the kindred, L. In. 76; Th. i. 150, 17: L. Ath. i. 2; Th. i. 200, 7. Ealle of &aelig-acute;gðere m&aelig-acute;gþe, L. E. G. 13; Th. i. 174, 21. Se slaga wille bétan wið m&aelig-acute;gþe, L. Edm. S. 7; Th. i. 250, 15. Gebéte wið ða m&aelig-acute;gþe, L. C. S. 39; Th. i. 398, 27: L. Edm. S. 4; Th. i. 248, 25. III. in a wider sense, descendants of a common ancestor living at the same time, a generation:--Ðé ic geseah sóðlíce rihtwísne ætforan mé on ðissere m&aelig-acute;gþe te enim vidi justum coram me in generatione hac, Gen. 7, 1. On ealræ m&aelig-acute;gþe in omni generatione, Ps. Spl. 44, 19. Hwí is áwriten on ðære béc Genesis ðæt Abrahames cynn sceolde gecyrran ongeán fram Aegypta lande on ðære feórþan m&aelig-acute;gþe and seó óðer bóc Exodus sægþ ðæt hí férdon of Aegyptan lande on ðære fíftan m&aelig-acute;gþe? . . Gif ðú telst ða m&aelig-acute;grace fram Iudan ðonne findst ðú ð&aelig-acute;r fíf m&aelig-acute;gþa, and gif ðú telst fram Leui ðonne findst ðú ð&aelig-acute;r feówer mægþa, Boutr. Scrd. 22, 16-20: Homl. Th. ii. 458, 34. Noe wæs rihtwís wer on his m&aelig-acute;gþum Noe vir justus fuit in generationibus suis, Gen. 6, 9: 9, 12. IV. with wider limits than those implied by family, (a) a tribe, subdivision of a people:--M&aelig-acute;gþ tribus, Wrt. Voc. 72, 48: Ælfc. Gr. 11; Som. 15, 23. Gegaderiaþ eów tó m&aelig-acute;gþum [and gange] ðæt gehlot fram m&aelig-acute;gþe tó m&aelig-acute;gþe and be manna híwr&aelig-acute;denum accedetis singuli per tribus vestras, et quamcumque tribum sors invenerit, accedit per cognationes suas, Jos. 7, 14. Of Asseres m&aelig-acute;gþe de tribu Asser, Lk. Skt. 2, 36. Leóda m&aelig-acute;gþe the tribes of men, Cd. 80; Th. 100, 16; Gen. 1665. Ðæra m&aelig-acute;gþa ealdras principes tribuum, Num. 1, 4. Of ðám twelf m&aelig-acute;gþum, 13, 3: Blickl. Homl. 155, 30. (b) a people, nation:--Ðære m&aelig-acute;gþe monwísan the manners of the people (of Sodom), Cd. 92; Th. 116, 20; Gen. 1939. Ná dyde hé swylc &aelig-acute;lcre m&aelig-acute;gþe non fecit taliter omni nationi, Ps. Spl. 147, 9: 49, 7. Gebannan manigre m&aelig-acute;gþe geond ðisne middangeard, Beo. Th. 150; B. 75. Ðonne hé ys tóweard on micelre m&aelig-acute;gþe and ða strengstan m&aelig-acute;gþe nú ealra eorþan m&aelig-acute;gþ beóþ on him gebletsode cum futurus sit in gentem magnam ac robustissimam et benedicendæ sint in illo omnes nationes terræ, Gen. 18, 18. Fremde þeóde, óðre m&aelig-acute;gþe, Ps. Th. 88, 43. Hæfdon ða m&aelig-acute;gþa &aelig-acute;lcne for écne god the nations held each to be god eternal, Bt. Met. Fox 26, 98; Met. 26, 49. M&aelig-acute;gþa tída tempora nationum, Lk. Skt. 21, 24: Cd. 124; Th. 158, 12; Gen. 2616: Beo. Th. 49; B. 25: 9; B. 5. (c) as in the case of proper names the word for the people is used for their country, so province, country:--Seó m&aelig-acute;gþ West-Seaxna provincia occidentalium Saxonum, Bd. 3. 7; S. 529, 2. Seó ylce m&aelig-acute;geþ &aelig-acute;rest ðysne biscop ágenne onféng hunc primum eadem provincia proprium accepit praesulem, 4, 12; S. 581,
' Uu
658 MÆGÞA -- M&AElig-acute;LAN.
24. Willferþ bisceop Súþ-Seaxna m&aelig-acute;gþe (provinciæ), 4, 13; S. 581, 37. From Armoricano ðære m&aelig-acute;geþe, 1, 1; S. 474, 7. Mid his m&aelig-acute;gþe Eást-Englum, 2, 15; S. 518, 27. On Beornicia m&aelig-acute;gþe, 2, 14; S. 518, 14. Hé férde geond ealle Angelcynnes m&aelig-acute;gþe perlustrans universa, 4. 2; S. 566, I. Him twá m&aelig-acute;gþe (duas provincias) forgeaf, 4, 13; S. 582, 10. Ða m&aelig-acute;gþe ðe mon háteþ Gallia Belgica, 1, 1; S. 473, 12. On Palestina ðære m&aelig-acute;gþe, Shrn. 100, 26. On Tiro ðære m&aelig-acute;gþe, Th. Ap. 3, 24: Blickl. Homl. 211, 16: Andr. Kmbl. 528; An. 264. [Orm. off Asæress ma&yogh;&yogh;þe.] v. fæderen-, folc-, ge-, médren-, súþ-, wer-m&aelig-acute;gþ.
mægþa, an; m. Maithen, may-weed; anthemis cotula :-- Mægþa herba putida, Ælfc. Gl. 42; Som. 64, 11; Wrt. Voc. 31, 22 : caluna ( = calmia, v. Lchdm. ii. 398, col. 2), 39; Som. 63, 71; Wrt. Voc. 30, 19. Him mon mægþan tó mete gegyrede, Lchdm. iii. 34, 11. v. mageþe.
Mægþa land the Polish province of Mazovia (?) :-- Be norþan Horiti is Mægþa land; and be norþan Mægþa londe Sermende óþ ða beorgas Riffen, Ors. l, l; Swt. 16, 21.
mægþ-, mægep-blæd, es; n. Pudendum muliebre :-- Mægeþblædd virginal, Germ. 400, 8. Leo 508, 9 says on this word 'Dieselbe Bedeutung hat Blatt noch in der deutschen Jägersprache: das Blatt einer Ricke, einer Hinde.'
mægþ-bót. e; f. The fine to be paid by an unmarried woman :-- Mægþbót sí swá friges mannes lei the fine to be paid by an unmarried woman be the same as that by a free man (for the same offence), L. Ethb. 74 j Th. i. 20, 9. This regulation follows one that settles the fine to be paid by 'frí wíf locbore.'
mægþ-, mægeþ-hád, es; m. I. maidenhood, virginity, celibacy, chastity :-- Ðú cennest cyning ealra cl&aelig-acute;nnessa and ðinne mægþhád nó ne gewemmest, Blickl. Homl. 7, 36: Exon. 12 a; Th. 18, 25; Cri. 289: 9 a; Th. 6, 16; Cri. 85 : Homl. Th. i. 460, 4. Mægþhád is &aelig-acute;gðer ge on w&aelig-acute;pmannum ge on wífmannum. Ða habbaþ rihtne mægþhád ða ðe fram cildháde wuniaþ on cl&aelig-acute;nnesse, 148, 13. Mæigþhád, 7. Ðæt sindan ða ða ðe mid wífum ne beóþ besmitene, and hira mægeþhád habbaþ gehealdenne, Past. 52, 7; Swt. 409, 7. Mæ[g]þhádes virginitatis, puritatis, Hpt. Gl. 411, 32: castitatis, 441, 69 : celibatus, pubertatis, 453, 56. Hé sceal foresceáwian ðam m&aelig-acute;dene hire mægþhádes wurþ (pretium pudicitiæ), Ex. 21, 10: L. Alf. 12; Th. i. 46, 18. Án man ðe sý mægþhádes man, cnapa oððe mægden, Herb. 104, 2; Lchdm. i. 218, 21. Hire meiþhádes pupertatis sue, Kent. Gl. 26. Ic bidde ðé for Scam. Marian mægþháde, Bt. Fox 260, 3. II. a body of young persons :-- Mægeþháde pedagogio, Wrt. Voc. ii. 77, 30. [Marh. meiðhad: Orm. ma&yogh;&yogh;þhadd: O. H. Ger. magad-heit virginitas, pubertas, coelibatus.] v. mægden-hád.
m&aelig-acute;gþ-hád, es; m. Kinship, relationship :-- 'Se ðe his brðdor ne lufaþ hé wunaþ on deáþe.' Ealle wé sind gebróðra ðe on God gelýfaþ and we ealle cweþaþ 'Úre Fæder þe eart on heofonum.' Ne gedyrstl&aelig-acute;ce nán man be m&aelig-acute;gþháde bútan sóðre lufe 'he who loveth not his brother continueth in death' ... All we are brethren that believe on God, and we all say 'our Father that art in heaven.' Let no man presume on kinship without true love. Homl. Th. i. 54, 6-11.
mægþhád-líc; adj. Virgin, virginal :-- Mæg[þ]hádlícre sidefulnysse pudicitiæ virginalis, Hpt. Gl. 440, 65.
m&aelig-acute;gþ-lagu = m&aelig-acute;g-lagu q.v., L.C.E.V; Th. i. 362, 28.
m&aelig-acute;gþ-leás; adj. Belonging to no family, not of distinguished family; ignobilis, Wrt. Voc. ii. 138, 73.
mægþ-mann, es; m. A maiden, virgin :-- Gif man mægþman néde genimep if a maiden be carried off by force (to be married), L. Ethb. 82 ; Th. i. 24, 3. v. mægden-mann.
m&aelig-acute;gþ-sibb, e; f. Kindred :-- M&aelig-acute;gþsybbe parentelæ, Hpt. Gl. 523, 10. v. m&aelig-acute;g-sibb.
m&aelig-acute;g-tudor, es; n. That which is produced from the same stock :-- M&aelig-acute;gtuðre cognatæ, Hpt. Gl. 469, 52. Cf. magu-tudor.
m&aelig-acute;g-wine, es; m. A kinsman and friend :-- Mon mænig be his m&aelig-acute;gwine many a man standing by his kinsman (of the people at the tower of Babel), Cd. 80; Th. 100, 9; Gen. 1661. M&aelig-acute;gwinas míne, Beo. Th. 4951; B. 2479. M&aelig-acute;gwinum. Cd. 149; Th. 187, 4; Exod. 146: 158; Th. 197, 28; Exod. 314: Salm. Kmbl. 719; Sal. 359. [O. Sax. mág-wini.]
m&aelig-acute;g-, még-wlite, es; m. Appearance, form, species; species, forma, aspectus :-- Mégwlit aspectus, Mt. Kmbl. Lind. 28, 3. M&aelig-acute;gwlit (mégwlitt, Rush) onsióne his species vultus ejus, Lk. Skt. Lind. 9, 29. Tó m&aelig-acute;gwlite andgytes ad formam sensus, Bd. 5, 24; S. 647, 34. Ðæt ðú meahte mínum weorþan m&aelig-acute;gwlite gelíc, Exon. 28b; Th. 87, 30; Cri. 1433. Gedyde ic ðæt ðú onsýn hæfdest, m&aelig-acute;gwlite mé gelícne, 28 a; Th. 84, 35; Cri. 1384: Andr. Kmbl. 1711; An. 858. Ne mégulit (mégwlit, Rush.) his geségon neque speciem ejus vidistis, Jn. Skt. Lind. 5, 37. Mégwlite, Rtl. 2, 7. Mégewlit Godes majestatem Dei, 1, 19. Mon ne m&aelig-acute;ge ða lástas on óðerne m&aelig-acute;gwlite oncyrran; ah hié á beóþ on ðære ilcan onsýne the footsteps cannot be changed into another form; but they always appear the same, Blickl. Homl. 127, 19. &AElig-acute;lc hafaþ mágwlite metodes and engla. Cd. 75; Th. 92, 17; Gen. 1530. Monge m&aelig-acute;gwlitas many species, Exon. 433; Th. 146, 7; Gú. 706; Bt. Met. Fox 31, 9; Met. 31, 5. Woroldgife monige on misenlícum m&aelig-acute;gwlitan dona in diversis speciebus perplura, Bd. 1, 32; S. 498, 21.
m&aelig-acute;gwlitian to form, shape :-- Oferhiuad ł [ofer] mégwlitgad transfiguratus. Mt. Kmbl. Lind. 17, 2.
m&aelig-acute;gwlit-líce; adv. Figuratively :-- Mégwlitlíce figuraliter, Mk. Skt. p. 4, 10.
mæhe (for mæhte?) dicione, Wrt. Voc. ii. 27, 75.
mæht, mæhtig. v. meaht, meahtig.
m&aelig-acute;l, mál, mél, es; n. m. (?) I. a measure :-- Dó wines þrié mél on pour three measures of wine on, L.M. 1, 45; Lchdm, ii. 110, 26. v. cucler-m&aelig-acute;l, dæg-m&aelig-acute;l, fot-m&aelig-acute;l, m&aelig-acute;l-tange; and cf. Icel. mál a measure: Dan. maal. II. a mark, sign, cross, crucifix :-- Hér ðþiéwde reád Cristes m&aelig-acute;l on hefenum in this year a red cross appeared in the sky. Chr. 773; Erl. 52, 23. Mid ðám wæs sum mycel gylden Cristes m&aelig-acute;l in quibus crucem magnam auream, Bd. 2, 20; S. 522, 9. Hé ðæt Cristes m&aelig-acute;l hræde weorce geworhte . . and ðæt Cristes m&aelig-acute;l genam and on ðone seáþ sette, 3, 2; S. 524, 16-18. B&aelig-acute;ron Cristes róde tácen sylfrene Cristes m&aelig-acute;l crucem pro vexillo ferentes argenteam, 1, 25; S. 487, 3. &AElig-acute;nne sylfrene mále on V. pundon a silver crucifix of five pounds, Chart. Th. 558, 33. Ðon on ealdan Cristes m&aelig-acute;le; of ðam Cristes m&aelig-acute;le, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. vi. 66, 34. Ealle hit writen mid Cristes m&aelig-acute;l all signed it with a cross, Chr. 963; Erl. 123, 25. v. fýr-m&aelig-acute;l, ge-m&aelig-acute;l, gr&aelig-acute;g-m&aelig-acute;l: O. Sax. hobid-m&aelig-acute;l head on a coin and cf. Icel. mál applied to the inlaid ornamenting of weapons: and English hring-, wunden-m&aelig-acute;l. The word is also used for the sword itself brogden m&aelig-acute;l, Beo. Th. 3236; B. 1616: 3338; 8. 1667: Elen. Kmbl. 1574; El. 759. v. mal-sweord. III. fixed, suitable, appointed time, season, occasion :-- M&aelig-acute;l is mé tó féran it is time for me to go, Beo. Th. 637; 316. Ðá wæs s&aelig-acute;l and m&aelig-acute;l ðæt tó healle gang Healfdenes sunu, 2021; B. 1008. Ðá ðæs m&aelig-acute;les wæs mearc agongen then was the appointed time past, Cd. 83; Th. 103, 16; Gen. 1719: 224; Th. 296, 12; Sat. 501. Ic ðæt m&aelig-acute;l geman ðonne we gehéton ússum hláforde I remember the time when we promised our lord, Beo. Th. 5259; B. 2633. Ælce m&aelig-acute;le on each occasion, Exon. 119a; Th. 457, 30; Hy. 4, 92. Se geweald hafaþ s&aelig-acute;la and m&aelig-acute;la he hath power over times and seasons. Beo. Th. 3226; 1611. Efne swylce m&aelig-acute;la swylce ... just at such times as ..., 2502; B. 1249. M&aelig-acute;la gehwylce on every occasion, 4121; B. 2057: Ps. Th. 118, 62. Ðú him mete sylest m&aelig-acute;la gehwylce and ðæs tídlíce tíd gemearcast tu das escam illis in tempore opportuno, 144, 16: 21. Ðæt &aelig-acute;r feala m&aelig-acute;la behýded wæs which long before was hidden, Elen. Kmbl. 1971; El. 987. &AElig-acute;rran m&aelig-acute;lum on former occasions, Beo. Th. 1819; B. 907: 4466; B. 2237: 6062; B. 3035. IV. the time for eating, a meal :-- Ðás hálgan lenctenlíce tide gehealdan mid cl&aelig-acute;num fæstene ælce dæge tó ánes m&aelig-acute;les (having only one meal a-day, cf. Icel. fasta einmælt). Wulfst. 285, 2. Hé gereordade æt ánum m&aelig-acute;le fif þúsend manna he fed at one (meal) time five thousand men, 293, 27. Yfel biþ ðæt man rihtfæstentíde &aelig-acute;r m&aelig-acute;le ete, L. C. S. 47; Th. i. 402, 24: Homl. Th. ii. 590, 25. Gífernys biþ ðæt se man &aelig-acute;r tíman hine gereordige oððe æt his m&aelig-acute;le tó micel þicge it is greediness when a man eats before the time or takes too much at his meal, 218, 30. Ne fæsþ se no Gode ac him selfum se ðe ðæt nyle þearfum sellan ðæt hé ðonne on m&aelig-acute;le l&aelig-acute;fþ ac wile hit healdan eft tó óðrum m&aelig-acute;le non Deo, sed sibi quisque jejunat, si ea quæ ventri ad tempus subtrahit, non egenis tribuit sed . . custodit, Past. 43, 8; Swt. 317, 4. Múþa gehwylc mete þearf m&aelig-acute;l sceolon tídum gongan every mouth needs meat; meals must there be at times, Exon. 91 a; Th. 341, 13; Gn. Ex. 125. [Laym. Orm. mæl: O. E. Homl. A. R. mel: Chauc. mel, meel a meal: Prompt. Parv. meel pastus: Goth. mél a time: Icel. mál time, meal-time, season: O. H. Ger. mál time, occasion: M. H. Ger. mál: Ger. ein-mal, etc.: M. H. Ger. mál time for eating, meal: Ger. mahl.] v. -m&aelig-acute;lum.
m&aelig-acute;l, e; f. A speech, talk, conversation :-- Gemuna ða m&aelig-acute;la ðe wé oft æt meodo spr&aelig-acute;con think of the talks that we oft had at table, Byrht. Th. 137, 66; By. 212. [Icel. mál; n. speech, colloquy, talk.] v. m&aelig-acute;lan.
m&aelig-acute;l, es; n. A cause, suit, action (?) :-- Ðú symle furðor feohtan sóhtest m&aelig-acute;l ofer mearce thou didst ever press on to fight, didst pursue thy cause (i.e. carry on war) over the border, Wald. 1, 33; Vald. l, 19. Cf. Icel. mál a suit, cause; sækja mál to prosecute (as a law term). Stephens takes m&aelig-acute;l here = mark, goal: Rieger (quoted by Grein) takes it = gemót, concio, so figuratively battle, v. mál.
m&aelig-acute;lan; p. de To speak :-- Se stán m&aelig-acute;lde for mannum the stone spake before men, Andr. Kmbl. 1533; An. 768. Wícinga ár wordum m&aelig-acute;lde, Byrht. Th. 132, 35; By. 26: 133, 1; By. 43: 137, 63; By. 210. Hyre se feónd oncwæþ, wordum m&aelig-acute;lde. Exon. 70 b; Th. 263, 18; Jul. 351. Be eów Essaias for weorodum wordum m&aelig-acute;lde, Elen. Kmbl. 702; El. 351. Him ða tó wuldorgást wordum m&aelig-acute;lde, Cd. 141; Th. 176, 16; Gen. 2913. Him Andreas wið, wine þearfende, wordum m&aelig-acute;lde, Andr. Kmbl. 600; An. 300. Him ðá tógénes ða gleáwestan wordum m&aelig-acute;ldon, Elen. Kmbl. 1072; El. 537. Hwæt mé God on mínum módsefan m&aelig-acute;lan wille quid loquatur in me dominus, Ps. Th. 84, 7. [Orm. mælenn: Havel, mele: Icel. mæla to speak.] v. ge-, on-m&aelig-acute;lan.
m&aelig-acute;lan to mark. [Goth. meljan to write: O. Sax. málon to mark (of
M&AElig-acute;LAN -- M&AElig-acute;R-APELDRE. 659
a wound made by a sword): O. H. Ger. málón, málén pingere: Ger. malen to paint.] v. hring-, scír-m&aelig-acute;led; m&aelig-acute;l II.
m&aelig-acute;lan to spot, blemish, v. ge-m&aelig-acute;lan, mál, un-m&aelig-acute;le.
m&aelig-acute;l-cearu, e; f. Care or trouble belonging to a particular time :-- Swá ða m&aelig-acute;lceare maga Healfdenes singala seáþ so did Healfdene's son ever brood over the trouble of that time, Beo. Th. 380; B. 189.
m&aelig-acute;l-dæg, es; m. A day, season, an appointed time :-- Hé ðæs m&aelig-acute;l-dæges self ne wénde ðæt him Sarra bringan meahte on woruld sunu he himself never hoped for the day when Sarah could bring him a son into the world, Cd. 107; Th. 141, 4; Gen. 2339. Hé moncynnes m&aelig-acute;ste hæfde on ð&aelig-acute;m m&aelig-acute;ldagum mægen and strengo, 79; Th. 98, 18; Gen. 1632.
m&aelig-acute;l-dropa, an; m. Phlegm :-- M&aelig-acute;ldropa. flegma. i. saliva, Wrt. Voc. ii. 149, 39.
m&aelig-acute;l-dropiende phlegmatic; flegmaticus, Ælfc. Gl. 77; Som. 72, 13; Wrt. 45, 47.
Mældún MALDON in Essex, Chr. 913; Erl. 102, 5: 920; Erl. 104, 32: 993; Erl. 132, 5.
m&aelig-acute;le spotted, v. un-m&aelig-acute;le.
m&aelig-acute;l-gesceaft, e; f. That which happens at its appointed time in accordance with the decrees of fate :-- Ic bád m&aelig-acute;lgesceafta I waited for that which in due time fate would assign me, Beo. Th. 5467; B. 2737.
m&aelig-acute;l-mete, es; m. Food to eat :-- Ne biþ ðec m&aelig-acute;lmete nymþe mores græs no food shall there be for thee but the grass of the moor. Cd. 203; Th. 252, 7; Dan. 575. [Grein, quoting Dietrich, would read m&aelig-acute;l méte ( = obvius), v. Hpt. Zeitsch. x. 358.]
m&aelig-acute;l-sceafa, an; m. A canker :-- M&aelig-acute;lscæafa eruca, Ælfc. Gl. 23; Som. 60, 3; Wrt. 24, 7. M&aelig-acute;lsceafa caniglata. Wrt. Voc. ii. 128, 19. M&aelig-acute;lsceafa eruca, Wrt. Voc. 78, 66; Zup. 310, 5. In the last reference one MS. (v. Wrt. Voc. 91, 23) has mæslesceafe; in Wrt. Voc. 161, 23 maseles translates rugeroles (see also Skeat's Dict. s. v. measles'), so m&aelig-acute;l, in this word, would mean a spot.
m&aelig-acute;l-tange, an; f. -tang, es; m. (?) A pair of compasses :-- M&aelig-acute;ltange circinum, Ælfc. Gl. 49; Som. 65, 70; Wrt. Voc. 34, 5: 62; Som. 68, 78; Wrt. Voc. 39, 61. M&aelig-acute;ltanges prica centrum, 39, 62.
-m&aelig-acute;lum -meal (in piece-meal), v. æcer-, bit-, d&aelig-acute;l-, drop-, flocc-, folc-, fót-, heáp-, híd-, lim-, nam-, sceáf-, stæp-, stund-, stycce-, þrag-, þreát-, þúsend-, worn (wearn)-, wræd-m&aelig-acute;lum.
m&aelig-acute;nan; p. de To mean. I. of persons (a) to intend to convey a certain sense :-- Gif hé of wege &aelig-acute;nigne gebrohte . . ðæt is ðæt ic m&aelig-acute;ne gif hé &aelig-acute;nigne man on synne bespeóne if he have brought any man out of the way . . . , what I mean, is, if he have lured any man to sin, L. Pen. 16; Th. ii. 284, 12. Hwet m&aelig-acute;nde Crist ðá cwæþ; 'Ða unrihtwísan faraþ on &aelig-acute;ce wítu,' Shrn. 197, 18. God ðá geopenude Abrahame hwæt hé mid ðære spr&aelig-acute;ce m&aelig-acute;nde. Gen. 18, 20. (b) to intend to indicate a certain person or thing without direct statement :-- Cweþan swá he tó ánum sprece and hwæðre ealle m&aelig-acute;neþ to say, as if he speaks to one and yet means all. Exon. 283; Th. 84, 24; Cri. 1378. Hé gecýðde ðæt hé ne m&aelig-acute;nde (indicaret) ðis andwearde lif, Past. 50, 2; Swt. 389, 22. Hwylc beren m&aelig-acute;nde hé ðonne elles búton heofona ríce, Blickl. Homl. 39, 27. Crist m&aelig-acute;nde ðone écan deáþ . . . ða Iudéiscan m&aelig-acute;ndon ðisne and-weardan deáþ. Homl. Th. ii. 232, 20. Ne m&aelig-acute;nde úre Drihten mid ðisum wordum ða treówa ðe on appeltúne wexaþ, 406, 9. (c) to mean, purpose, have as an object to which the mind is directed, intend :-- Gif hé ðara nán ne déþ ðonne nát hé hwæt hé ménþ (Cott. MS. mænþ) if he does none of these, then he does not know what he means, Bt. 38, 2; Fox 198, 28. Ðá ongon hé sprecan swíðe feorran ymbútan swilce hé ná ða spr&aelig-acute;ce ne m&aelig-acute;nde, 39, 5] Fox 218, 12. Hwæt ðú ðonne m&aelig-acute;ne mid ðære gítsunge ðæs feós what do you mean by the greed of money? 32, 1; Fox 114, 7. II. (of things) to signify, have a certain signification or purpose :-- Saga hwæt ic m&aelig-acute;ne, Salm. Kmbl. 472 ; Sal. 236: Exon. 124 b; Th. 479, 18; Rä. 62, 9. Oft gehwá gesihþ fægre stafas and nát hwæt hí m&aelig-acute;naþ, Homl. Th. i. 186, 3. Hwæt m&aelig-acute;nde ðæt syxtig wera strongera? Blickl. Homl. 11, 22: Homl. Th. ii. 234, 31. Faraþ and leorníaþ hwæt ðæt m&aelig-acute;ne: 'Ic wylle mildheortnysse, and ná offrunge,' 470, 18. Geleornian hwæt fulluht m&aelig-acute;ne. Wulfst. 123, 4. Understandan hwæt ða twá word m&aelig-acute;nan, abrenuntio and credo, 38, 8. [O. Sax. ménian: O. Frs. ména: O. H. Ger. meinian : Ger. meinen.] v. ge-m&aelig-acute;nan.
m&aelig-acute;nan; p. de To tell of, relate, declare :-- Ne wyrneþ word lofes, wísan m&aelig-acute;neþ mine for mengo (cf. O. Sax. thú fora thesaro thiod telis, mahtig ménis). Exon. 105b; Th. 401, 14; Rä. 21, 11. Hæleþ hý hospe m&aelig-acute;naþ men speak of her contemptuously, 90 a; Th. 337, 17; Gn. Ex. 66. Secgas nemnaþ, m&aelig-acute;naþ mid múþe meodugáles gedrinc, 88 a; Th. 330, 26; Vy. 57. Ðý læs ðæt weras gieddum m&aelig-acute;ndan be mé lifgendum lest men should tell of it in songs during my lifetime, 50 b; Th. 176, 9; Gú. 1206, Ic mæg singan and secgan, spell m&aelig-acute;nan, hú me cynegóde cystum dohten, 85 b; Th. 321, 32 ; Wid. 55: Beo. Th. 2139; B. 1067. Ð&aelig-acute;r wæs Beówulfes m&aelig-acute;rþo m&aelig-acute;ned there was told Beowulf's greatness, 1718; B. 857. [O. Sax. ménian, gi-ménian to make known: O. H. Ger. meinian dicere: ga-meinian dicere, dicare, Grff. ii. 785, 788.]
m&aelig-acute;nan; p. de To lament, mourn, complain. I. intrans. :-- Ðú simle mid wópe and mid unrótnesse m&aelig-acute;nst gif ðé &aelig-acute;nies willan wana biþ (tu) qui abesse aliquid tuae beatitudini tam luctuosus atque anxius conqueraris, Bt. II, 1; Fox 30, 22. Ðá hé gehiérde ðæt ðæt folc mænde tó him Arone ymb hiera earfeðo Moyses cum contra se et Aaron conqueri populum cognovisset, Past. 28, 6; Swt. 201, 4. Ealle wordum m&aelig-acute;ndon, Cd. 222: Th. 288, 24; Sae. 386. II. followed by a clause :-- Da welan ðe dú m&aelig-acute;ndest ðæt ðú forlure the wealth which you complain of having lost, Bt. 7, 3; Fox 20, 18. Bonan m&aelig-acute;ndon ðæt hý monnes bearn oferþunge, Exon. 38b; Th. 128, 8; Gú. 401. III. with acc. :-- Hú Boetius his earfoðu tó Gode m&aelig-acute;nde, Bt. tit. cap. 4. His tungan hé m&aelig-acute;nde swíðost he complained most of his tongue, Homl. Th. i. 330, 31. Basilius ménde ðæt unriht, Homl. Skt. 3, 322. Hé misbeád his munecan and ða munecas hit m&aelig-acute;ndon lufelíce, Chr. 1083; Erl. 217, 4. Hi m&aelig-acute;ndon mondryhtnes cwealm they mourned their lord's death, Beo. Th. 6289; B. 3149. Ic wundrige hwæt ðé seó oððe hwæt ðú m&aelig-acute;ne admiror cur aegrotes. Bt. 5, 3; Fox 12, 11. Hú miht ðú m&aelig-acute;nan ðæt wyrse nú ðú ðæt leófre hæfst gehealden poterisne, meliora quæque retinens, de infortunio jure caussari? 10; Fox 28, 10. Cyning m&aelig-acute;nan to mourn their king. Beo. Th. 6324; B. 3172. Ic gehére gnorniende cynn grundas m&aelig-acute;nan (the devils in hell), Cd. 216; Th. 273, 10; Sat. 134. Ðæt ic sceal teárum m&aelig-acute;nan that I must mourn with tears. Exon. 76a; Th. 285, 10; Jul. 712. v. bem&aelig-acute;nan.
m&aelig-acute;ne; adj. I. mean, wicked, false, evil :-- Synna lustas m&aelig-acute;ne módlufan the pleasures of sin, vicious love, Exon. 71 a; Th. 364, 26; Jul. 370. Hygeleáse m&aelig-acute;ne mad and false (the rebel angels), Cd. 4; Th. 4, 11; Gen. 52. Þurh m&aelig-acute;nra hand searonettum beseted. Andr. Kmbl. 1882 ; An. 943. II. the word however occurs most often in reference to oaths :-- Se ðe his þances m&aelig-acute;nne áþ swerige and hé wite ðæt hé m&aelig-acute;ne biþ æfter ðam qui sua sponte perjuraverit et postea scit quod perjurus est, L. Ecg. C. 34; Th. ii. 158, 20, 14, 16. Gif hwá swereþ and se áþ beó m&aelig-acute;ne . . se ðe m&aelig-acute;ne áþas begá si quis juraverit et perjurium sit. . . Qui perjuria commiserit, L. Ecg. P. iv. 68; Th. ii. 228, 7-9: L. Edg. C. 8; Th. ii. 262, 31. Gif mæssepreóst stande on leásre gewitnesse oððe on m&aelig-acute;nan áþe if a masspriest be concerned in false witness or perjury, L. Eth. ix. 27; Th. i. 346, 9 : L. C. E. 5 ; Th. i. 362, 30. Se ðe mánáþ (other MS. m&aelig-acute;nne áþ) swerige, L. Ath. i. 25; Th. i. 212, 18. Be m&aelig-acute;nan áþe. Gif hwá m&aelig-acute;ne áþ swerige, L. C. S. 36; Th. i. 398, 3-4. Gebéte ðone m&aelig-acute;nan áþ, L. In 35; Th. i. 124, 13. Swerian m&aelig-acute;nne áþ þurh swá miclan mægenþrymme. Wulfst. 214, 15. Eall yfel forl&aelig-acute;tan ge on manslihte ge on m&aelig-acute;num áþum, 228, 21. v. un-m&aelig-acute;ne; mán.
m&aelig-acute;ne; adj. Common :-- M&aelig-acute;na l&aelig-acute;se common pasturage. Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iv. 284, 8. v. ge-m&aelig-acute;ne.
mængan, Mæn-íg, mænig, mænigeo, mænnisc. v. mengan, mon-íg, manig, menigu, mennisc.
maenoe. v. mene.
m&aelig-acute;nsumian; p. ode. I. to have the companionship of a person, to marry :-- Ne hiá m&aelig-acute;nsumiaþ (m&aelig-acute;nsumigaþ, Rush.) ne hiá biþon gem&aelig-acute;nsumad (i. ne ceorl hæfis wífes gemána ne wíf hæfis ceorles) neque nubent neque nubentur, Mk. Skt. Lind. 12, 25. II. to share with another, to communicate :-- Ménsumede participavit, communicavit. Hpt. Gl. 467,
m&aelig-acute;nsumung, e; f. I. communion, admission to fellowship with others (opp. of excommunication) :-- Benedictus cwæþ ðæt hí unámánsumode w&aelig-acute;ron . . . Hi underféngon ða hálgan m&aelig-acute;nsumunge æt Gode þurh his þeówan Benedicte, Homl. Th. ii. 174, 31. II. participation :-- Hé ús forgeáfe d&aelig-acute;l on his ríce, and m&aelig-acute;nsumunge on his godcundnysse, i. 140, 11.
mæntel. v. mentel.
mær. v. wudu-mær.
mæra, mera, an; m. An incubus :-- Mera ł satyrus incuba, Ep. Gl. 12 f, 14. v. mære.
m&aelig-acute;r-ác, e; f. An oak which serves as part of a boundary (?) :-- Of ðære ác in ða m&aelig-acute;rác, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iii. 379, 31. v. m&aelig-acute;r-bróc, mearc-béce.
m&aelig-acute;ran, máran; p. de To make known, celebrate, declare, proclaim :-- Mín múþ sægeþ ðíne mægenspéde and ðín sóþfæst weorc m&aelig-acute;reþ os meum pronuntiabit justitiam tuam, Ps. Th. 70, 14. Songe lofiaþ m&aelig-acute;raþ módigne meaglum reordum they praise with song and with powerful voices celebrate the noble bird, Exon. 60b; Th. 221, 21; Ph. 338. For cyning m&aelig-acute;raþ leófne leódfruman they proclaim the loved chief as king, Th. 222, 6; Ph. 344. Swylce mín tunge tídum m&aelig-acute;rde ðín sóþfæst weorc sed et lingua mea tota die meditabitur justitiam tuam, Ps. Th. 70, 22. Ðæt hí heora bearnum budun and sægdun and cinn óðrum cýðden and m&aelig-acute;rden ut notam faceret eam fliis suis; ut cognoscat generatio altera, 77, 7. Gé scyldigra synne secgaþ, sóþfæstra nó mód and monþeáw m&aelig-acute;ran willaþ, Exon. 40a; Th. 132, 26; Gú. 478. Hit n&aelig-acute;nig mon út cýðan ne móste, ðý læs ða elreordigan kyningas on ðæt f&aelig-acute;gon, ðæt ic swá lytle hwíle lifgean móste. Ne hit &aelig-acute;nig mon ðære ferde ðon má út máran móste, ðý læs hié for ðon ormóde w&aelig-acute;ron, Nar. 32, 22. [Goth. mérjan to proclaim, announce: O. Sax. márian; Icel. mæra to praise: O. H. Ger. márian diffamare, declarare, clarificare, praedicare.] v. ge-m&aelig-acute;ran.
m&aelig-acute;r-apeldre, an; f. An apple-tree which serves as a boundary :-- Hit cymeþ tó m&aelig-acute;rapeldran, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iii. 390, 5.
660 M&AElig-acute;R-BRÓC -- M&AElig-acute;RSIAN.
m&aelig-acute;r-bróc, es; in. A brook which forms a boundary, cf. mearc-bróc :-- Tó m&aelig-acute;rbróce; of m&aelig-acute;rbróce, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iii. 79, 5: 438, 27: v. 284, 29 (where mér-bróc is the same as merc-bróc of l. 13). v. mere and m&aelig-acute;re a boundary.
mærc. v. mearc, mearh.
m&aelig-acute;r-dic, e; f. A boundary dike :-- On ða m&aelig-acute;rdíc, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iii. 378, 24. On ða ealdan m&aelig-acute;rdíc, 449, 10.
mære a mere, v. mere.
mære, mare, mere, an; f. A night-mare, a monster oppressing men during sleep (cf. passage quoted in Cl. and Vig. under mara; 'En er hann hafði litt sofnat, kallaði hann ok sagði at mara trað hann. Menn hans fóru til, ok vildu hjálpa honum; en er þeir tóku uppi til höfuðsins, þá trað hón fótleggina swá at nær brotnuðu. Þá tóku þeir til fótanna, þá kafði hón höfuðit, svá at þar dó hann') :-- Mære faecce, Wrt. Voc. ii. 108, 44: incuba, 111, 46. Mere fecce, 35, 26. Gif mon mare ríde, L. M. 1, 64; Lchdm. ii. 140, 9. Hi beóþ góde wið nihtgengan and maran, 3, 1; Lchdm. ii. 306, 12. [Prompt. Parv. mare or ny&yogh;hte mare epialtes; mare or wyche magus, maga, sagana, and see note, p. 326: Icel. mara: M. H. Ger. mare: Ger. mahr: cf. French cauchemar.] v. mær, mæra.
m&aelig-acute;re, es; n. A boundary, limit, confine, border :-- Ondlong ðæs m&aelig-acute;res (meres?) heges, Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iii. 32, 30: ii. 250, 7(?). In m&aelig-acute;re Judéana in fines Judaea, Mt. Kmbl. Rush. 19, 1. In m&aelig-acute;rum in villas, Mk. Skt. Lind. 6, 56. In m&aelig-acute;rum (m&aelig-acute;ro, Rush.) in vicos, Lk. Skt. Lind. 14, 21. [Cf. Icel. mærr a border-land.] v. ge-m&aelig-acute;re m&aelig-acute;r-ác, -apeldre, -bróc, -díc, -heg, -stán, -þorn, -weg.
m&aelig-acute;re; adj. Great, excellent, distinguished, illustrious, sublime, splendid, celebrated, famous, widely known (of persons or things) :-- Mære clarus, insignis, nobilis, perspicuus, Wrt. Voc. ii. 131, 66: inclytus, 46, 10, 11. Mere weard percrebuit, Ep. Gl. 18b, 10. M&aelig-acute;re celeber, Ælfc. Gr. 9, 18; Zup. 44, 10. M&aelig-acute;rne celebre, Hpt. Gl. 525, 45. Beorht ł m&aelig-acute;re præclara, splendida, 436, 43. M&aelig-acute;r[re] illustrius, 460, 25. I. (of persons and (a) in a good sense) :-- Dryhten ys m&aelig-acute;re God and mihtig Dominus est deus magnus et potens. Deut. 10, 17. Ðú eart m&aelig-acute;re God, and Jacobes God se m&aelig-acute;ra, Ps. Th. 83, 8 : 103, 23. God m&aelig-acute;re (excelsus) álýsend heora is. Ps. Spl. 77, 39. Freá ælmihtig, m&aelig-acute;re þeóden, Cd. 40; Th. 52, 34; Gen. 853. Se m&aelig-acute;ra Fæder (God), L. Ælfc. C. 3; Th. ii. 344, 4. Hé byþ m&aelig-acute;re beforan Drihtne erit magnus coram domino. Lk. Skt. 1. 15: 32. Ðeáh he on ðam lande seó m&aelig-acute;re ðonne biþ hé on óðrum unm&aelig-acute;re though he be famous in one country, he is not in another, Bt. 30, 1; Fox 108, 15. Wæs hé (St. Martin) swíðe m&aelig-acute;re geond middangeard, Blickl. Homl. 221, 1. M&aelig-acute;ru cwén the illustrious queen (Wealhtheow), Beo. Th. 4037; B. 2016. Sunu se ðe biþ góde m&aelig-acute;re a son (Isaac) who shall be great in goodness, Cd. 100; Th. 133, 24; Gen. 2198: Beo. Th. 3909; B. 1952. Mihtum m&aelig-acute;re great in power, Elen. Kmbl. 679; El. 340. Marian m&aelig-acute;rre meówlan. of Mary, maiden illustrious, Exon. 14 a; Th. 28, 13; Cri. 446. Smeágende cwidas and d&aelig-acute;da ðara m&aelig-acute;rena (illustrium) wera úre þeóde, Bd. pref.; S. 471, 13. Ðes ys m&aelig-acute;rra (major) ðonne ðæt templ, Mt. Kmbl. 12, 6. Nis betwux wífa bearnum nán m&aelig-acute;rra wítega ðonne Johannes, Lk. Skt. 7, 28. Nán man ne biþ for óðres góde nó ðý m&aelig-acute;rra ne nó ðý geheredra splendidum te aliena claritudo non efficit. Bt. 30, 1; Fox 108, 27. David wæs hearpera m&aelig-acute;rost, Ps. C. 50; Ps. Grn. ii. 276, 4. Ðás mán&dash-uncertain;fullan men w&aelig-acute;ron getealde for ða m&aelig-acute;rostan godas, Wulfst. 106, 17. (b) in a bad sense, notorious, distinguished by evil deeds; insignis :-- Hæfdum énne gebundenne m&aelig-acute;rne (mérne. Lind.) monn se wæs háten Barrabas (cf. O. Sax. mári meginthiof) habebat vinctum insignem qui dicebatur Barabbas, Mt. Kmbl. Rush. 27, 16. Grendel, m&aelig-acute;re mearc-stapa, Beo. Th. 206; B. 103: 1528; B. 762 (?). II. (of things) :-- Sum deófolgild ðe mid ð&aelig-acute;m h&aelig-acute;ðenum mannum swíðe weorþ and m&aelig-acute;re wæs a certain idol that was held in high honour and esteem among the heathens, Blickl. Homl. 221, 7. Swíðe m&aelig-acute;re burh se is háten Sepontus a very famous town which is called Sepontus, 197, 20. On ðam m&aelig-acute;ran (inlustri) túne, se is nemned æt Walle, Bd. 3, 21; S. 551, 11: Cd. 205; Th. 254, 10; Dan. 609. Tó ðære m&aelig-acute;ran byrig (the heavenly Jerusalem), 227; Th. 304, 4; Sat. 624. Tempel heáhst and háligost, hæleþum gefr&aelig-acute;gost, m&aelig-acute;st and m&aelig-acute;rost (Solomon's temple), 162; Th. 202, 28; Exod. 395. Ðæt wæs ðæt m&aelig-acute;reste hús ðe on eorþan geworht wurde that (the temple) was the most splendid house that was built in the world. Wulfst. 278, 1. M&aelig-acute;re wurdon his wundra geweorc wíde and síde far and wide spread the fame of the wonders he wrought. Exon. 45 b; Th. 155, l; Gú. 853. Eall ðeós m&aelig-acute;re gesceaft the universe. Rood Kmbl. 24; Kr. 12. M&aelig-acute;re wundur mirabilia, Ps. Th. 106, 30: 110, 3. Sunne m&aelig-acute;re tungol the sun, resplendent star. Chr. 937; Erl. 112, 14; Æðelst. 14. M&aelig-acute;rost tungla, Exon. 57 b; Th. 205, 28; Ph. 119. In dege mérum in die insigni, Ps. Surt. 80, 4. Ðone m&aelig-acute;ron symbeldæg Drihtnes upstige, Blickl. Homl. 131, 10: Cd. 8; Th. 10, II; Gen. 155. Seó m&aelig-acute;re tiid (Easter), Menol. Fox 114; Men. 57. Se m&aelig-acute;ra dæg the great and terrible day of the Lord, Exon. 23 b; Th. 65, 16; Cri. 1055. Ðæt is m&aelig-acute;re spell no common tale is that, Cd. 119; Th. 155, 2; Gen. 2566: Elen. Kmbl. 1936; El. 970. Æfter ðisse d&aelig-acute;de his noma wæs weorþ and m&aelig-acute;re geworden after this deed his name became honoured and famous, Blickl. Homl. 219, 4-: Exon. 1073; Th. 409, 11; Rä. 27, 27. Is wuldur ðín wíde and síde ofer ðás eorþan ealle m&aelig-acute;re in omnem terram gloria tua. Ps. Th. 56, 6. Se m&aelig-acute;resta hlísa fama celeberrima, Bd. 3, 13: S. 538, 37. Ðæt is m&aelig-acute;ro wyrd that is a tremendous event (the deluge), Cd. 69; Th. 84, 18; Gen. 1399. Ðín mægen is swá m&aelig-acute;re, swá ðæt &aelig-acute;nig ne wát eorþbúende ða deópnesse Drihtnes mihta, Hy. 3, 31; Hy. Grn. ii. 282, 31. (In a bad sense) Caudenes Furcules seó stów gewearþ swíðe m&aelig-acute;re for Rómána bismere Caudinas furculas satis celebres et famosas Romanorum fecit infamia, Ors. 3, 8; Swt. 120, 21. [Cf. Goth. waila-mérs of good report; wailaméreins good report: O. Sax. mári: Icel. mærr: O. H. Ger. mári memorabilis, famosus, illustris, insignis, clarus.] v. efen-, folc-, fore-, forþ-, freá-, fr&aelig-acute;-, heaðo-, un-, wíd-m&aelig-acute;re.
mære pure, in the phrase m&aelig-acute;re peningas = Lat. meri denarii i.e. coins made of pure silver, v. Ducange s.v. merus, quoted by Schmid. The passage in which the word is found occurs in L. Alf. pol. 3; Th. i. 62, 10 :-- Mid V. pundum m&aelig-acute;rra pæninga. With this may be compared the following passage :-- For his lícweorðan feó, ðæt is ii pund mérehwítes seolfres. Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iii. 255, 12.
m&aelig-acute;rels, márels, es; m. and m&aelig-acute;rels-ráp, es; m. A rope for mooring a ship; pronesium [v. Ducange: 'pronexium funis quo navis religatur ad palum'] :-- M&aelig-acute;relsráp pronesium, Ælfc. Gl. 105; Som. 78, 21; Wrt. Voc. 57. 3. Márels prosnesium, 63, 62. [Botn words occur in lists giving the names of ships, and their various parts. Cf. Du. marlijn, also marl-reep = mar-reep a marline, a small cord used for binding large ropes, to protect them: O. Du. maren to tie knots, which occurs in English in the phrase to moor a ship. Also cf. marly&n-long; illaqueo, marlyd illaqueatus, Prompt. Parv. 327, and note.] v. scip-m&aelig-acute;rels.
m&aelig-acute;re-torrit. v. mere-torht.
mærh. v. mearh.
m&aelig-acute;r-heg, es; m. A boundary (?) hedge :-- Ondlong ðære burnan óþ hit cymeþ tó ðæm m&aelig-acute;rhege; ondlong ðæs m&aelig-acute;res heges ðæt hit cymeþ up on ða dúne. Cod. Dip. Kmbl. iii. 32, 29. Cf. gem&aelig-acute;r-haga.
m&aelig-acute;r-hlísa, an; m. Great fame, celebrity :-- Mid m&aelig-acute;rhlísan cælebri, Wrt. Voc. ii. 23, 74.
m&aelig-acute;rian; p. ode To become great, be distinguished :-- Swá m&aelig-acute;re-gend[iend]um cýðere tanto prestanti martiri, Hymn. Surt. 46, 3.
mæring a plant name :-- Hwít mæringc (Cockayne suggests sweet basil), Lchdm. iii. 2, 21.
m&aelig-acute;r-líc; adj. Great, magnificent, glorious, splendid, illustrious (of persons or things) :-- M&aelig-acute;rlíce magnificas, Gl. Wülck. 254, 11. I. (of persons) :-- M&aelig-acute;rlíc (God) on hálignysse magnificus in sanctitate, Cant. Moys. 11. Ðæt wæter feóll ofer Pharaones m&aelig-acute;rlícum riddum the water fell upon Pharaoh's splendid knights, Ælfc. T. Grn. 5, 31. II. (of things) :-- Mýrlíc cynehelm corona inclita, Kent. Gl. 67. Gabrihel bodade Zacharian his m&aelig-acute;rlícan drohtnunge Gabriel announced to Zacharias his (John's) glorious life. Homl. Th. i. 352, 26. Ðá hæfde ðæt cild swíðe m&aelig-acute;rlíce stemne the boy had a magnificent voice, Wulfst. 152, 11.
